qs.q: Neither the principal nor the teachers _____ present at the emergency staff meeting yesterday.
qs.e: When two subjects are joined by 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the closer subject ('teachers', which is plural).

qs.q: Either the manager or his assistants _____ responsible for updating the daily register.
qs.e: With 'either... or', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it ('assistants', plural).

qs.q: The director, together with his senior officers, _____ attending the international conference in Geneva.
qs.e: Phrases like 'together with' do not make the subject plural; the singular subject 'director' requires the singular verb 'is'.

qs.q: Three-quarters of the farmland _____ been cleared for the upcoming planting season.
qs.e: Fractions take a singular verb when referring to an uncountable noun or a single unit of land ('farmland').

qs.q: Bread and butter _____ his primary breakfast option every morning.
qs.e: When two items combine to express a single idea or compound entity (like 'bread and butter' as a meal), a singular verb is used.

qs.q: Every student and teacher in the school _____ expected to attend the founder's day celebration.
qs.e: Nouns preceded by 'every' take a singular verb, even when joined by 'and'.

qs.q: Many a candidate _____ failed to read the examination instructions carefully.
qs.e: 'Many a' is followed by a singular countable noun and requires a singular verb.

qs.q: Neither of the two proposed solutions _____ acceptable to the union representatives.
qs.e: 'Neither of' followed by a plural noun takes a singular verb in standard English.

qs.q: The committee _____ reached a unanimous decision regarding the new policy.
qs.e: Collective nouns like 'committee' take a singular verb when the group acts as a single unified body.

qs.q: The jury _____ divided in their opinions regarding the guilt of the accused.
qs.e: Collective nouns take a plural verb when members of the group act individually or hold differing views.

qs.q: One of the boys who _____ always causing trouble in class has been suspended.
qs.e: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural antecedent 'boys', so the relative clause requires the plural verb 'are'.

qs.q: He is one of those employees who _____ consistently late to work.
qs.e: 'Who' refers to 'employees' (plural), requiring the plural verb 'are' in the relative clause.

qs.q: Either you or I _____ responsible for delivering the keynote address today.
qs.e: With 'either... or', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it ('I', requiring 'am').

qs.q: Neither he nor I _____ aware of the sudden change in the timetable.
qs.e: The verb agrees with the nearest subject ('I'), taking the singular past tense 'was'.

qs.q: The principal as well as the vice-principals _____ commended for the school's success.
qs.e: Parenthetical phrases introduced by 'as well as' do not alter the singular agreement dictated by the primary subject 'principal'.

qs.q: No student and no teacher _____ allowed into the laboratory without a protective coat.
qs.e: Singular subjects preceded by 'no' connected by 'and' take a singular verb.

qs.q: Physics _____ considered by many students to be a challenging subject.
qs.e: Academic subjects ending in '-s' like 'Physics' are singular in meaning and take singular verbs.

qs.q: Ten kilometers _____ a long distance to walk in the scorching sun.
qs.e: Amounts, distances, periods of time, and sums of money are treated as single quantities and take singular verbs.

qs.q: The cattle _____ grazing peacefully in the lush green valley.
qs.e: 'Cattle' is a plural noun that always takes a plural verb.

qs.q: The police _____ investigating the cause of the sudden outbreak of fire.
qs.e: 'Police' is a plural collective noun that takes a plural verb.

qs.q: Measles _____ a contagious viral disease that primarily affects children.
qs.e: Diseases ending in '-s' like 'measles' take a singular verb.

qs.q: A number of students _____ waiting outside the principal's office for their transcripts.
qs.e: The expression 'a number of' takes a plural verb, whereas 'the number of' takes a singular verb.

qs.q: The number of qualified applicants _____ increased dramatically this year.
qs.e: The phrase 'the number of' is singular and takes the singular verb 'has'.

qs.q: None of the stolen money _____ recovered by the police detectives.
qs.e: 'None' takes a singular verb when referring to an uncountable noun ('money').

qs.q: None of the missing books _____ returned to the school library.
qs.e: 'None' takes a plural verb when referring to a plural countable noun ('books').

qs.q: All the spilled oil _____ washed away by the heavy rain.
qs.e: 'All' takes a singular verb when referring to an uncountable noun ('oil').

qs.q: All the candidates _____ seated before the commencement of the examination.
qs.e: 'All' takes a plural verb when referring to plural countable nouns ('candidates').

qs.q: Statistics _____ a required course for all social science undergraduates.
qs.e: When 'statistics' refers to the branch of study, it takes a singular verb.

qs.q: The statistics _____ that youth unemployment has declined slightly.
qs.e: When 'statistics' refers to numerical data or facts, it takes a plural verb.

qs.q: A pair of scissors _____ left on the tailor's cutting table.
qs.e: The subject 'pair' is singular, so it takes the singular verb 'was'.

qs.q: The scissors _____ dull and need to be sharpened before use.
qs.e: Plural tools like 'scissors' take a plural verb when used without 'a pair of'.

qs.q: More than one candidate _____ interviewed for the vacant position.
qs.e: 'More than one' takes a singular noun and a singular verb.

qs.q: The news broadcast by the international station _____ encouraging.
qs.e: 'News' is an uncountable singular noun and takes a singular verb.

qs.q: The poultry _____ fed twice daily by the farm hands.
qs.e: 'Poultry' when referring to the birds collectively takes a plural verb.

qs.q: Twenty thousand naira _____ the total amount required for registration.
qs.e: Sums of money take a singular verb as they represent a single quantity.

qs.q: By the time the fire brigade arrived, the building _____ completely burned down.
qs.e: The past perfect tense 'had' is required to indicate an action completed before another past action.

qs.q: If I _____ known about the change in schedule, I would have informed you earlier.
qs.e: Third conditional sentences require the past perfect ('had known') in the if-clause.

qs.q: She has been working in this medical research facility _____ five years.
qs.e: 'For' is used to denote a duration of time, whereas 'since' denotes a specific starting point.

qs.q: He had barely sat down when the telephone _____ ringing loudly.
qs.e: Clauses introduced by 'barely... when' take the simple past tense in the dependent clause.

qs.q: I would rather you _____ at home tonight as the roads are unsafe.
qs.e: The expression 'would rather' followed by a clause taking a subject requires the simple past subjunctive form.

qs.q: It is high time the government _____ effective measures against inflation.
qs.e: 'It is high time' is followed by a past subjunctive verb form to indicate present urgency.

qs.q: The earth _____ around the sun in an elliptical orbit.
qs.e: General truths and scientific facts are expressed in the simple present tense.

qs.q: She promised that she _____ send the document as soon as she arrived.
qs.e: In indirect speech anchored in the past ('promised'), future 'will' changes to conditional 'would'.

qs.q: When the teacher entered the classroom, the students _____ an exercise.
qs.e: The past continuous tense is used for an action that was ongoing when another past action occurred.

qs.q: By next month, the contractor _____ the construction of the bridge.
qs.e: The future perfect tense ('will have completed') expresses an action that will be finished before a specified future time.

qs.q: If it rains heavily tomorrow morning, the football match _____ postponed.
qs.e: First conditional sentences express real future possibilities using present simple in the condition and 'will' in the main clause.

qs.q: If I were the president of the union, I _____ the welfare scheme.
qs.e: Second conditional sentences use 'were' in the if-clause and 'would' + base verb in the main clause.

qs.q: Unless you study diligently, you _____ pass the upcoming examinations.
qs.e: 'Unless' means 'if not' and takes a future real condition structure.

qs.q: I wish I _____ where he hid the key yesterday afternoon.
qs.e: Unfulfilled wishes about the past require the past perfect tense ('had known').

qs.q: He talks about international politics as if he _____ an ambassador.
qs.e: 'As if' introducing a hypothetical condition takes the past subjunctive 'were'.

qs.q: Before she moved to the capital city, she _____ in a quiet rural town.
qs.e: Past perfect 'had lived' indicates a state that existed prior to another past event ('moved').

qs.q: Scarcely had the speaker stepped on stage when the audience _____ cheering.
qs.e: 'Scarcely... when' constructions require simple past in the main clause following the past perfect inversion.

qs.q: The morning express train _____ from platform four every day at six o'clock.
qs.e: Scheduled routines and timetables are stated in the simple present tense.

qs.q: They _____ for the missing passenger for over three hours now.
qs.e: Present perfect continuous is used for actions starting in the past and continuing up to the present moment.

qs.q: As soon as the referee blew the whistle, the players _____ off the pitch.
qs.e: Actions occurring sequentially in the past both use the simple past tense.

qs.q: She acts as though she _____ the owner of the entire establishment.
qs.e: Hypothetical present situations introduced by 'as though' require the past subjunctive 'were'.

qs.q: I _____ my former school principal since we graduated three years ago.
qs.e: 'Since' connecting a past point to the present requires the present perfect tense in the main clause.

qs.q: While the chef was preparing the main meal, his assistants _____ the salad.
qs.e: Parallel ongoing actions in the past both take the past continuous tense.

qs.q: The suspect admitted that he _____ the safe two nights before.
qs.e: Reported past events prior to the reporting verb require the past perfect tense.

qs.q: If she _____ the instructions carefully, she would not have made those mistakes.
qs.e: Third conditional required 'had read' in the condition clause.

qs.q: Supposing you _____ a million dollars, how would you spend it?
qs.e: 'Supposing' introducing a hypothetical present/future scenario takes the simple past verb ('won').

qs.q: It is time the municipal council _____ the damaged street lights.
qs.e: 'It is time' takes a simple past verb form to express present necessity.

qs.q: I would prefer that he _____ the report directly to the board tomorrow.
qs.e: Preferences introduced by 'would prefer that' take the subjunctive base form 'submit'.

qs.q: By this time next week, we _____ our final semester examinations.
qs.e: Future continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at a specific future moment.

qs.q: She _____ in a quiet village before relocating to the metropolis.
qs.e: 'Used to' expresses a habitual past state or action that no longer exists.

qs.q: He _____ early every morning because his job starts at seven.
qs.e: 'Be used to' followed by a gerund expresses familiarity with a current habit.

qs.q: No sooner _____ the news than she broke down in tears.
qs.e: 'No sooner' at the beginning of a sentence requires auxiliary inversion ('had she heard').

qs.q: The committee requested that the secretary _____ the minutes immediately.
qs.e: Verbs of command or request ('requested that') take the present subjunctive base form 'circulate'.

qs.q: If water is heated to one hundred degrees Celsius, it _____.
qs.e: Zero conditional scientific facts take simple present in both clauses.

qs.q: He walked into the room silently lest he _____ the sleeping infant.
qs.e: 'Lest' is followed by 'should' + base verb in formal English.

qs.q: The prisoner was acquitted _____ all charges owing to lack of sufficient evidence.
qs.e: The verb 'acquitted' takes the preposition 'of' when referring to charges or crimes.

qs.q: Senior citizens are not immune _____ the financial effects of rising inflation.
qs.e: The adjective 'immune' is followed by the preposition 'to'.

qs.q: She is severely allergic _____ peanuts and all types of tree nuts.
qs.e: 'Allergic' is idiomatic with the preposition 'to'.

qs.q: The official dropped a subtle hint _____ his intention to resign at the end of the year.
qs.e: 'Hint' as a verb or noun indicating indirect reference takes 'at'.

qs.q: The manager insisted _____ reviewing all financial statements before signing the agreement.
qs.e: The verb 'insist' is followed by the preposition 'on' (or 'upon').

qs.q: All contractors must strictly comply _____ the safety regulations established by the board.
qs.e: 'Comply' requires the preposition 'with'.

qs.q: New students often find it difficult to adapt _____ the rigorous academic routine.
qs.e: The verb 'adapt' takes the preposition 'to' when referring to adjusting to conditions.

qs.q: Pedestrians were advised to refrain _____ crossing the highway outside designated zones.
qs.e: 'Refrain' requires the preposition 'from' followed by a gerund.

qs.q: The school board congratulated the principal _____ her outstanding leadership award.
qs.e: One congratulates someone 'on' an achievement or occasion, not 'for'.

qs.q: My grandfather prefers traditional tea _____ sweetened carbonated drinks.
qs.e: The verb 'prefer' takes 'to' when comparing two items.

qs.q: We are all looking forward _____ meeting the renowned author at the book launch.
qs.e: 'Look forward to' is a phrasal verb where 'to' is a preposition followed by a gerund.

qs.q: The suspect was accused _____ embezzling public funds allocated for road construction.
qs.e: The verb 'accuse' takes the preposition 'of'.

qs.q: The driver was charged _____ reckless driving and endangerment of human life.
qs.e: The verb 'charge' (legal context) takes the preposition 'with'.

qs.q: You cannot rely entirely _____ internet search engines for rigorous academic research.
qs.e: 'Rely' requires the preposition 'on' or 'upon'.

qs.q: Our success in the tournament depends _____ how well the team coordinates its defense.
qs.e: The verb 'depend' takes the preposition 'on'.

qs.q: All participants are required to abide _____ the rules set by the organizing committee.
qs.e: 'Abide by' means to accept and obey a decision or rule.

qs.q: Members of the jury must abstain _____ discussing the trial outside the courtroom.
qs.e: 'Abstain' takes the preposition 'from'.

qs.q: The court found the motorist guilty _____ driving under the influence of alcohol.
qs.e: 'Guilty' takes the preposition 'of'.

qs.q: Hard work and perseverance remain the fundamental keys _____ sustainable success.
qs.e: 'Key' in this metaphorical sense takes 'to'.

qs.q: Engineers have proposed an innovative solution _____ the urban traffic congestion problem.
qs.e: 'Solution' takes the preposition 'to'.

qs.q: Margarine is often used as a substitute _____ butter in commercial baking recipes.
qs.e: 'Substitute' takes the preposition 'for'.

qs.q: The archer aimed carefully _____ the center of the target before releasing the arrow.
qs.e: The verb 'aim' takes the preposition 'at'.

qs.q: The principal does not approve _____ students leaving the premises during break hours.
qs.e: 'Approve' in the sense of sanctioning or liking takes 'of'.

qs.q: Travelers in the region were warned to beware _____ fraudulent ticket vendors.
qs.e: 'Beware' takes the preposition 'of'.

qs.q: The committee consists _____ ten independent experts drawn from various universities.
qs.e: 'Consists of' means to be composed or made up of.

qs.q: His peaceful public persona contrasts sharply _____ his aggressive private conduct.
qs.e: 'Contrast' as a verb takes 'with'.

qs.q: She found it difficult to cope _____ the overwhelming demands of her new executive post.
qs.e: The correct phrasal expression is 'cope with' (not 'cope up with').

qs.q: His personal opinions differ significantly _____ those expressed by his political party.
qs.e: 'Differ' takes the preposition 'from' when denoting unlikeness.

qs.q: The young mathematician excels _____ solving complex differential equations.
qs.e: 'Excel' takes the preposition 'in' (or 'at').

qs.q: He glanced quickly _____ his wristwatch during the lengthy introductory address.
qs.e: 'Glance' takes the preposition 'at'.

qs.q: The director objected _____ making any compromises on the safety specifications.
qs.e: 'Object' as a verb takes the preposition 'to' followed by a gerund.

qs.q: Heavy security measures prevented unauthorized visitors _____ entering the server room.
qs.e: 'Prevent' takes 'from' + gerund.

qs.q: The photograph reminded the elderly woman _____ her happy childhood in the countryside.
qs.e: 'Remind' takes 'of' when evoking a memory.

qs.q: After years of diligent preparation, she finally succeeded _____ passing the board exam.
qs.e: 'Succeed' takes the preposition 'in' + gerund.

qs.q: The young man was absorbed _____ his reading and did not notice the passage of time.
qs.e: 'Absorbed' meaning deeply engrossed takes 'in'.

qs.q: You hardly ever visit your former classmates these days, _____?
qs.e: Negative words like 'hardly' make the statement negative, requiring a positive tag ('do you').

qs.q: Let us proceed to the next item on our meeting agenda, _____?
qs.e: Statements beginning with 'Let us / Let's' take the tag 'shall we'.

qs.q: Nobody was injured in the highway collision, _____?
qs.e: 'Nobody' is negative and takes a plural pronoun 'they' in the positive tag ('were they').

qs.q: She can barely walk without the support of a crutch, _____?
qs.e: 'Barely' makes the clause negative, so the question tag must be positive ('can she').

qs.q: Shut the main gate before leaving the compound, _____?
qs.e: Imperative requests take 'will you' or 'would you' as their tag.

qs.q: I am responsible for coordinating the sports festival, _____?
qs.e: The standard informal/spoken question tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I'.

qs.q: Everyone has submitted their completed assignment, _____?
qs.e: Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone' take the plural pronoun 'they' in the question tag.

qs.q: You had better see a medical specialist regarding that cough, _____?
qs.e: The tag for 'had better' uses the auxiliary 'hadn't' ('hadn't you').

qs.q: He used to train at the local gymnasium every morning, _____?
qs.e: The auxiliary verb 'did' is used for question tags following 'used to'.

qs.q: Nothing was damaged during the severe thunderstorm, _____?
qs.e: 'Nothing' is singular and negative, taking the positive tag 'was it'.

qs.q: Somebody left a leather briefcase in the reception area, _____?
qs.e: 'Somebody' takes the plural pronoun 'they' in the negative question tag ('didn't they').

qs.q: Neither of the candidates performed satisfactorily in the interview, _____?
qs.e: 'Neither' makes the statement negative, requiring a positive plural tag 'did they'.

qs.q: You would rather stay at home than attend the party, _____?
qs.e: The auxiliary in 'would rather' is 'would', forming the tag 'wouldn't you'.

qs.q: Let me assist you with those heavy parcels, _____?
qs.e: Imperative requests directed at helping someone take 'will you'.

qs.q: Do not make any noise in the examination hall, _____?
qs.e: Negative imperatives take the positive tag 'will you'.

qs.q: She seldom complains about her heavy workload, _____?
qs.e: The negative adverb 'seldom' requires a positive tag ('does she').

qs.q: Few students managed to score above eighty percent, _____?
qs.e: 'Few' has a negative meaning ('almost none'), requiring a positive tag ('did they').

qs.q: A little patience is required when dealing with toddlers, _____?
qs.e: 'A little' is positive in meaning, requiring a negative tag ('isn't it').

qs.q: Little hope remains for finding any survivors in the rubble, _____?
qs.e: 'Little' has a negative sense, requiring a positive tag ('does it').

qs.q: There is no point in arguing over spilled milk, _____?
qs.e: Existential 'there' statements with negative 'no point' take 'is there'.

qs.q: There are several issues that need urgent attention, _____?
qs.e: Existential 'there are' positive statements take 'aren't there'.

qs.q: She needs to work much harder to improve her grades, _____?
qs.e: When 'need' functions as a main verb, it forms its tag with 'do/does' ('doesn't she').

qs.q: He dare not challenge the authority of the managing director, _____?
qs.e: When 'dare' functions as a modal auxiliary, its tag uses 'dare' ('dare he').

qs.q: You ought to pay your taxes promptly, _____?
qs.e: The formal question tag for 'ought to' is 'oughtn't you' (or 'shouldn't you').

qs.q: That is the book you were searching for all morning, _____?
qs.e: Demonstratives 'that/this' take the pronoun 'it' in question tags ('isn't it').

qs.q: These are the results of the annual health survey, _____?
qs.e: Demonstratives 'these/those' take the pronoun 'they' in question tags ('aren't they').

qs.q: He has a vast collection of antique coins in his study, _____?
qs.e: In modern standard English, main verb 'has' forms question tags with 'does/doesn't' ('doesn't he').

qs.q: They had a pleasant vacation at the coastal resort, _____?
qs.e: Main verb 'had' forms its question tag with 'did/didn't' ('didn't they').

qs.q: You have completed all the assigned laboratory exercises, _____?
qs.e: Auxiliary 'have' in the present perfect forms the tag 'haven't you'.

qs.q: Let's organize a cleanup campaign for our neighborhood, _____?
qs.e: 'Let's' invariably takes the question tag 'shall we'.

qs.q: Hardly had the aircraft touched down _____ one of its tires burst suddenly.
qs.e: 'Hardly had...' is idiomatically completed by 'when'.

qs.q: No sooner had the chief speaker taken his seat _____ the applause broke out.
qs.e: 'No sooner had...' is idiomatically completed by 'than'.

qs.q: Scarcely had the match begun _____ rain started pouring heavily.
qs.e: 'Scarcely had...' pairs with 'when'.

qs.q: Barely had the police arrived at the scene _____ the robbers fled into the bush.
qs.e: 'Barely had...' pairs with 'when'.

qs.q: _____ the heavy downpour, the outdoor sports competition continued as scheduled.
qs.e: 'In spite of' (or 'despite' without 'of') takes a noun phrase.

qs.q: _____ she prepared thoroughly for the interview, she was not selected for the role.
qs.e: 'Although' introduces a subordinate clause containing a subject and verb.

qs.q: You will not be allowed into the examination hall _____ you present your registration card.
qs.e: 'Unless' means 'if not' and introduces a condition.

qs.q: The company agreed to fund the project _____ the committee submitted quarterly reports.
qs.e: 'Provided that' means 'on condition that'.

qs.q: Take an umbrella with you _____ it rains unexpectedly later in the afternoon.
qs.e: 'In case' indicates preparation for a possible future event.

qs.q: He spoke in low whispers _____ he should disturb the sleeping patients in the ward.
qs.e: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and takes 'should' or subjunctive.

qs.q: She studied relentlessly _____ she might secure a full scholarship to the university.
qs.e: 'So that' expresses purpose and is followed by 'might/may/can'.

qs.q: It was _____ a fascinating story that I read the entire book in one sitting.
qs.e: 'Such a + adjective + noun + that' expresses degree and result.

qs.q: The music was _____ loud that conversation inside the hall became impossible.
qs.e: 'So + adjective + that' expresses degree and result.

qs.q: Not only did he win the marathon, _____ he also broke the national record.
qs.e: 'Not only... but also' is a correlative conjunction pair.

qs.q: You must either pay the full fee today _____ forfeit your reservation.
qs.e: 'Either' pairs with 'or'.

qs.q: Neither the minister _____ his deputy was available to receive the petition.
qs.e: 'Neither' pairs with 'nor'.

qs.q: Both the principal _____ the vice-principal attended the regional educational summit.
qs.e: The correlative conjunction 'both' is always completed by 'and' to join the two elements: both X and Y. None of the other options completes the pair correctly.

qs.q: He could not decide _____ to accept the job offer in the capital or stay locally.
qs.e: 'Whether... or' presents alternatives.

qs.q: You can choose _____ course suits your career ambitions best.
qs.e: 'Whichever' is used when selecting from a limited number of choices.

qs.q: _____ hard he tried, he could not loosen the rusty iron bolt.
qs.e: 'However' + adjective/adverb expresses concession ('no matter how').

qs.q: The dog followed its owner _____ he went around the spacious compound.
qs.e: 'Wherever' means in or to whatever place.

qs.q: While the eldest son chose engineering, the younger son preferred fine arts, _____ the daughter studied law.
qs.e: 'Whereas' introduces a contrast between two facts.

qs.q: _____ it is raining outside, we had better stay indoors and read.
qs.e: 'Since' introduces a cause or reason equivalent to 'because'.

qs.q: Now _____ you have completed your degree, what are your future career plans?
qs.e: 'Now that' means 'since' or 'seeing that' regarding a newly present fact.

qs.q: _____ you have admitted your mistake, no further disciplinary action will be taken.
qs.e: 'Seeing that' introduces an established fact serving as a reason.

qs.q: Inasmuch _____ the company has met its sales targets, bonuses will be distributed.
qs.e: 'Inasmuch as' is a formal conjunction meaning 'considering that' or 'since'.

qs.q: He saved his earnings diligently in order _____ he could purchase his own farmland.
qs.e: 'In order that' introduces a purpose clause containing a subject and verb.

qs.q: The lecture was postponed owing _____ the sudden illness of the guest speaker.
qs.e: 'Owing to' means 'because of' and requires 'to'.

qs.q: He was disqualified on the grounds _____ he had falsified his age documents.
qs.e: 'On the grounds that' introduces the reason for an action.

qs.q: In the event _____ rain, the prize presentation ceremony will be held indoors.
qs.e: 'In the event of' takes a noun phrase to express a future contingency.

qs.q: Between you and _____, the newly appointed department head lacks managerial experience.
qs.e: Prepositions like 'between' govern the objective case ('me').

qs.q: The track star runs much faster than _____, though we train together.
qs.e: In formal English after comparative 'than', 'I' is the subject of the implied clause 'than I do'.

qs.q: It was _____ who organized the fundraising drive for the village health center.
qs.e: Predicate nominative after the linking verb 'was' takes the subjective pronoun 'he'.

qs.q: The committee decided to award the scholarship to whoever _____ the criteria best.
qs.e: 'Whoever' is the subject of the noun clause and takes the singular verb 'meets'.

qs.q: You may invite _____ you choose to attend the anniversary dinner.
qs.e: 'Whomever' functions as the object of 'you choose' in the subordinate clause.

qs.q: The driver _____ vehicle crashed into the railing was taken to the hospital.
qs.e: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun modifying 'vehicle'.

qs.q: Every student must ensure that _____ hall pass is displayed during school hours.
qs.e: Singular indefinite pronoun 'every student' formally requires a singular possessive ('his or her').

qs.q: One should always be careful with _____ public utterances during crisis moments.
qs.e: The pronoun 'one' takes the possessive 'one's' to maintain consistent pronoun reference.

qs.q: The mother cat licked _____ kittens gently to keep them clean and warm.
qs.e: 'Its' is the possessive form without an apostrophe.

qs.q: The young apprentice accidentally cut _____ while working with the sharp chisel.
qs.e: The correct reflexive pronoun for a male subject is 'himself'.

qs.q: After the fierce argument, the three business partners refused to speak to _____.
qs.e: 'One another' is preferred when referring to more than two persons.

qs.q: The two identical twin sisters always share their clothes with _____.
qs.e: 'Each other' is traditionally used when referring to two persons.

qs.q: To _____ was that formal letter of complaint addressed?
qs.e: Prepositions like 'to' require the objective pronoun 'whom'.

qs.q: The young researcher _____ received the national science award was praised by all.
qs.e: 'Who' is the subject of the relative clause 'received the award'.

qs.q: The woman _____ we met at the educational conference last week has published a new book.
qs.e: 'Whom' functions as the direct object of 'we met'.

qs.q: It is _____ who am responsible for maintaining the financial ledgers.
qs.e: Subject pronoun 'I' agrees with the verb 'am' in the relative clause.

qs.q: My elder brother and _____ spent the entire afternoon repairing the bicycle.
qs.e: Compound subject requires the subjective case 'I' ('brother and I').

qs.q: The school director presented the award directly to my classmate and _____.
qs.e: Direct object of the preposition 'to' requires the objective pronoun 'me'.

qs.q: The house _____ stood on the hill was completely destroyed by the landslide.
qs.e: Emphatic pronoun 'itself' reinforces the noun 'house'.

qs.q: None of the female candidates forgot _____ hall ticket for the examination.
qs.e: Singular reference to 'none' among female candidates takes possessive 'her'.

qs.q: Neither of the boys brought _____ physical education kit to school today.
qs.e: 'Neither' is singular and takes the singular possessive pronoun 'his'.

qs.q: Either of the two proposed policies has _____ distinct advantages and drawbacks.
qs.e: Singular 'either' takes the singular possessive pronoun 'its'.

qs.q: The author _____ works were cited in the article will deliver a lecture today.
qs.e: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun modifying 'works'.

qs.q: Who's responsible for making sure the doors are locked? Here 'Who's' means _____.
qs.e: 'Who's' is a contraction of 'Who is' (or 'Who has').

qs.q: The trophy was awarded to the team _____ displayed the highest sportsmanship.
qs.e: Relative pronoun 'that' or 'which' introduces a clause referring to a collective team.

qs.q: Of the two twin brothers, Peter is undoubtedly the _____.
qs.e: When comparing exactly two items or people, the comparative form ('taller') is used.

qs.q: Of all the students in the final year class, Grace is the _____ intelligent.
qs.e: When comparing more than two, the superlative form ('most') is required.

qs.q: The sprinter ran as _____ as he could to break the school record.
qs.e: 'Fast' functions as both an adjective and an adverb; 'fastly' does not exist.

qs.q: She has been working _____ all week to meet the project deadline.
qs.e: 'Hard' as an adverb means with great effort; 'hardly' means scarcely.

qs.q: He _____ ever attends social gatherings due to his introverted nature.
qs.e: 'Hardly' is an adverb of degree meaning scarcely or almost never.

qs.q: The international flight arrived two hours _____ than originally scheduled.
qs.e: 'Later' refers to time subsequent to a specified point.

qs.q: Have you heard any news from your elder brother _____?
qs.e: 'Lately' is an adverb meaning recently.

qs.q: Between the former proposal and the _____ option, I prefer the second one.
qs.e: 'Latter' refers to the second of two mentioned things.

qs.q: She bought a _____ leather jacket during her trip to Italy.
qs.e: Adjective order follows Opinion ('beautiful') -> Size ('small') -> Color ('black').

qs.q: The patient feels much _____ today after taking the prescribed medication.
qs.e: Double comparatives like 'more better' are grammatically incorrect; 'better' is modified by 'much'.

qs.q: This border post is the _____ point reached by our expedition team.
qs.e: 'Farthest' refers to measurable physical distance.

qs.q: For _____ details concerning the admission requirements, visit the portal.
qs.e: 'Further' refers to additional or non-physical extent.

qs.q: The guest speaker delivered his lecture so _____ that everyone understood.
qs.e: An adverb ('clearly') is required to modify the verb 'delivered'.

qs.q: She sings so _____ that she was selected to lead the school choir.
qs.e: 'Well' is the adverb modifying the verb 'sings'.

qs.q: The freshly baked loaves of bread smell extremely _____.
qs.e: Sense verbs like 'smell' take predicate adjectives ('delicious') rather than adverbs.

qs.q: The soup tastes _____ because the chef added too much salt.
qs.e: Linking verb 'tastes' is followed by the predicate adjective 'salty'.

qs.q: The chauffeur drove the luxury vehicle very _____ along the narrow mountain pass.
qs.e: Adverb 'carefully' modifies the action verb 'drove'.

qs.q: He was _____ an inspiring leader that everyone worked willingly.
qs.e: 'Such an + adjective + noun' is the correct structure.

qs.q: The weather was _____ pleasant that we decided to have a picnic.
qs.e: 'So + adjective + that' is the correct structure.

qs.q: There are _____ applicants for the position this year than last year.
qs.e: 'Fewer' is used with plural countable nouns ('applicants').

qs.q: There is _____ rainfall in the northern region during the dry season.
qs.e: 'Less' is used with uncountable nouns ('rainfall').

qs.q: He has received _____ valuable advice from his mentor over the years.
qs.e: 'Advice' is uncountable and is modified by 'much' or 'valuable'.

qs.q: My _____ brother has been practicing medicine for over fifteen years.
qs.e: 'Elder' is used specifically for family relationships.

qs.q: John is two years _____ than his closest friend in the class.
qs.e: 'Older' takes 'than' when comparing age generally.

qs.q: Take the _____ turning on your right after crossing the iron bridge.
qs.e: 'Next' refers to sequential order in direction.

qs.q: Direct: 'I will deliver the judgment tomorrow,' said the judge. Reported: The judge said that he _____ deliver the judgment the following day.
qs.e: Direct 'will' shifts to conditional 'would' in reported speech anchored in past.

qs.q: Direct: 'We are leaving for the airport now,' announced Mary. Reported: Mary announced that they _____ for the airport then.
qs.e: Present continuous 'are leaving' shifts to past continuous 'were leaving', and 'now' to 'then'.

qs.q: Direct: 'I have finished my project,' said Peter. Reported: Peter stated that he _____ his project.
qs.e: Present perfect 'have finished' shifts to past perfect 'had finished'.

qs.q: Direct: 'Where do you live?' asked the stranger. Reported: The stranger asked me where I _____.
qs.e: Reported questions use statement word order without auxiliary 'do' and shift tense to past ('lived').

qs.q: Direct: 'Did you see the eclipse yesterday?' asked Jane. Reported: Jane inquired if I _____ the eclipse the day before.
qs.e: Past simple in direct speech shifts to past perfect 'had seen' in reported speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'Do not open the door,' warned the guard. Reported: The guard warned us _____ the door.
qs.e: Negative imperatives shift to 'not to + verb' in indirect speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'The earth moves around the sun,' explained the teacher. Reported: The teacher explained that the earth _____ around the sun.
qs.e: Universal truths retain simple present tense in reported speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'I may attend the seminar,' said Susan. Reported: Susan mentioned that she _____ attend the seminar.
qs.e: Direct modal 'may' shifts to 'might' in reported speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'You must submit your papers today,' said the supervisor. Reported: The supervisor instructed us that we _____ submit our papers that day.
qs.e: Modal 'must' indicating obligation shifts to 'had to' in reported speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'Can you swim across the river?' asked the instructor. Reported: The instructor asked whether I _____ swim across the river.
qs.e: Direct 'can' shifts to 'could' in reported speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'I shall return these books next week,' said Samuel. Reported: Samuel said that he _____ return those books the following week.
qs.e: First person 'shall' expressing future intent shifts to 'would' for third person 'he'.

qs.q: Direct: 'What a beautiful painting this is!' exclaimed the visitor. Reported: The visitor exclaimed that it _____ a very beautiful painting.
qs.e: Direct exclamation 'is' shifts to past simple 'was'.

qs.q: Direct: 'Let us take a short break,' suggested the team leader. Reported: The team leader suggested that they _____ a short break.
qs.e: Suggestions with 'Let us' shift to 'suggested that + subject + should + verb'.

qs.q: Direct: 'Bring me a glass of water,' requested the old man. Reported: The elderly man requested me _____ him a glass of water.
qs.e: Direct imperative requests shift to 'to + infinitive' ('to bring').

qs.q: Direct: 'I visited the national museum last week,' said David. Reported: David mentioned that he had visited the national museum _____.
qs.e: Time expression 'last week' shifts to 'the previous week' or 'the week before'.

qs.q: Direct: 'These apples are fresh,' stated the vendor. Reported: The fruit vendor stated that _____ apples were fresh.
qs.e: Demonstrative 'these' shifts to 'those' in reported speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'I am writing an essay today,' said Grace. Reported: Grace explained that she was writing an essay _____.
qs.e: Time expression 'today' shifts to 'that day'.

qs.q: Direct: 'Will you attend the rehearsal tonight?' asked the director. Reported: The director asked if I _____ attend the rehearsal that night.
qs.e: Future question 'Will you' shifts to 'if I would'.

qs.q: Direct: 'I cannot solve this equation,' confessed Paul. Reported: Paul confessed that he _____ solve that equation.
qs.e: Direct 'cannot' shifts to 'could not' in indirect speech.

qs.q: Direct: 'We have been waiting here for two hours,' complained the passengers. Reported: The passengers complained that they had been waiting _____ for two hours.
qs.e: Adverb of place 'here' shifts to 'there' in reported speech.

qs.q: Active: 'The gale force winds destroyed several roofs in the community.' Passive: 'Several roofs in the community _____ by the gale force winds.'
qs.e: Simple past active ('destroyed') converts to plural past passive ('were destroyed').

qs.q: Active: 'The government is constructing a new bypass road.' Passive: 'A new bypass road _____ by the government.'
qs.e: Present continuous active converts to present continuous passive ('is being constructed').

qs.q: Active: 'The committee has approved the revised budget.' Passive: 'The revised budget _____ by the committee.'
qs.e: Present perfect active converts to present perfect passive ('has been approved').

qs.q: Active: 'They must submit the final project report by Friday.' Passive: 'The final project report _____ by Friday.'
qs.e: Modal auxiliary 'must' active converts to passive 'must be submitted'.

qs.q: Active: 'Someone stole my leather bag at the bus terminal.' Passive: 'My leather bag _____ at the bus terminal.'
qs.e: Simple past active converts to singular past passive ('was stolen').

qs.q: Active: 'The technician will repair the air conditioner tomorrow.' Passive: 'The air conditioner _____ by the technician tomorrow.'
qs.e: Simple future 'will repair' converts to future passive 'will be repaired'.

qs.q: Active: 'The police had caught the burglar before dawn.' Passive: 'The burglar _____ by the police before dawn.'
qs.e: Past perfect active 'had caught' converts to past perfect passive 'had been caught'.

qs.q: Active: 'People speak English in many countries around the world.' Passive: 'English _____ in many countries around the world.'
qs.e: Simple present active converts to present passive 'is spoken'.

qs.q: Active: 'The usher opened the doors at eight o'clock.' Passive: 'The doors _____ at eight o'clock by the usher.'
qs.e: Simple past active with plural object 'doors' converts to 'were opened'.

qs.q: Active: 'Clean the laboratory equipment after the experiment.' Passive: 'Let the laboratory equipment _____ after the experiment.'
qs.e: Imperative active converts to passive with 'Let... be cleaned'.

qs.q: Active: 'Who wrote this famous novel?' Passive: 'By whom _____ this famous novel written?'
qs.e: Passive interrogative form for past simple uses auxiliary 'was' ('By whom was...').

qs.q: Active: 'They are planting fruit trees along the fence.' Passive: 'Fruit trees _____ along the fence.'
qs.e: Present continuous active converts to plural present continuous passive 'are being planted'.

qs.q: Active: 'The board will review all applications next week.' Passive: 'All applications _____ by the board next week.'
qs.e: Future simple active converts to 'will be reviewed'.

qs.q: Active: 'The headmaster praised the hardworking pupil.' Passive: 'The hardworking pupil _____ by the headmaster.'
qs.e: Simple past active converts to singular past passive 'was praised'.

qs.q: Active: 'You should lock the office door before leaving.' Passive: 'The office door _____ before leaving.'
qs.e: Modal 'should' active converts to passive 'should be locked'.

qs.q: Which of the following sentences is correctly punctuated?
o: The rain stopped, however the ground remained slippery.
The rain stopped however; the ground remained slippery.
The rain stopped; however, the ground remained slippery.
The rain stopped however, the ground remained slippery.
qs.e: A semicolon is required before a conjunctive adverb like 'however' connecting two independent clauses, followed by a comma.

qs.q: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the apostrophe for possession.
o: The teacher's common room were renovated during the holidays.
The teachers common room was renovated during the holidays.
The teachers's common room was renovated during the holidays.
The teachers' common room was renovated during the holidays.
qs.e: Plural nouns ending in 's' take an apostrophe after the 's' to indicate possession ('teachers'').

qs.q: Which sentence correctly avoids a comma splice error?
o: He was exhausted from the journey; therefore, he went straight to bed.
He was exhausted from the journey, therefore he went straight to bed.
He was exhausted from the journey, he went straight to bed.
He was exhausted from the journey so, he went straight to bed.
qs.e: A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined by only a comma without a coordinating conjunction.

qs.q: Identify the sentence with correct colon punctuation.
o: The candidate needed three items: for the exam a pen, an eraser, and a ruler.
The candidate needed three items for the exam: a pen, an eraser, and a ruler.
The candidate needed: three items for the exam, a pen, an eraser, and a ruler.
The candidate needed three items for the exam, a pen: an eraser and a ruler.
qs.e: A colon is used to introduce an itemized list after a complete independent clause.

qs.q: Select the sentence with proper hyphenation.
o: The well known scientist delivered an inspiring lecture.
The well-known-scientist delivered an inspiring lecture.
The well-known scientist delivered an inspiring lecture.
The well known-scientist delivered an inspiring lecture.
qs.e: A compound adjective preceding the noun it modifies is hyphenated ('well-known scientist').

qs.q: Which sentence displays correct quotation punctuation?
o: 'Where are you going'? asked the mother.
'Where are you going,' asked the mother.
'Where are you going' asked the mother.
'Where are you going?' asked the mother.
qs.e: The question mark belongs inside the quotation marks when part of the direct speech.

qs.q: Identify the correctly capitalized title in a sentence.
o: We read 'The Mayor of Casterbridge' in our literature class.
We read 'The mayor of casterbridge' in our literature class.
We read 'the Mayor Of Casterbridge' in our literature class.
We read 'The Mayor Of Casterbridge' in our literature class.
qs.e: Major words in book titles are capitalized, while minor words like prepositions ('of') remain lowercase.

qs.q: Choose the sentence that correctly uses parentheses.
o: The annual report published last week (shows a significant profit).
The annual report (published last week) shows a significant profit.
The annual report (published last week shows) a significant profit.
The annual report published (last week shows a significant profit).
qs.e: Parentheses enclose supplementary or explanatory information within a complete sentence.

qs.q: Which sentence correctly distinguishes between 'its' and 'it's'?
o: The dog wagged it's tail because its happy to see it's owner.
The dog wagged its tail because its happy to see it's owner.
The dog wagged its tail because it's happy to see its owner.
The dog wagged it's tail because it's happy to see its owner.
qs.e: 'Its' is possessive, while 'it's' is a contraction for 'it is'.

qs.q: Select the sentence that avoids a run-on error.
o: She loves classical music her brother prefers modern jazz.
She loves classical music, her brother prefers modern jazz.
She loves classical music so her brother prefers modern jazz.
She loves classical music. Her brother prefers modern jazz.
qs.e: Two independent clauses must be separated into two sentences, joined by a semicolon, or connected with a coordinating conjunction.

qs.q: 'The committee was impressed by his 'meticulous' approach to resolving the dispute.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'meticulous' means attentive to detail. 'painstaking' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The witness gave a 'candid' account of what transpired during the incident.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'candid' means open and honest. 'frank' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The old man led a 'frugal' lifestyle despite his immense wealth.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'frugal' means economical with money. 'thrifty' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The company's initial profits showed an 'ephemeral' surge after the launch.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'ephemeral' means lasting a very short time. 'transient' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'She is a 'gregarious' individual who thrives in lively social gatherings.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'gregarious' means enjoying the company of others. 'sociable' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The board adopted a 'pragmatic' strategy to solve the budget deficit.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'pragmatic' means dealing with things sensibly and realistically. 'practical' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Mobile phones have become 'ubiquitous' in modern society.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'ubiquitous' means found everywhere. 'omnipresent' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'benevolent' donor provided full scholarships for ten indigent students.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'benevolent' means well-meaning and kindly. 'kindhearted' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The monk lived an 'austere' life in the secluded mountain monastery.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'austere' means severe or strict in manner. 'stern' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The professor offered a 'lucid' explanation of the complex theorem.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'lucid' means expressed clearly and easy to understand. 'clear' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'His 'audacious' plan to climb the steep cliff surprised his guides.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'audacious' means showing a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks. 'bold' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Additional evidence was brought in to 'bolster' the defense case.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'bolster' means support or strengthen. 'reinforce' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'We appreciated the diplomat's 'candor' during the delicate negotiation.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'candor' means the quality of being open and honest. 'honesty' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'docile' horse followed the trainer's commands without resistance.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'docile' means ready to accept control or instruction. 'submissive' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The painter's 'enigmatic' smile in the portrait intrigued art critics.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'enigmatic' means difficult to understand or mysterious. 'mysterious' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'He is 'fastidious' about maintaining absolute cleanliness in his kitchen.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'fastidious' means very attentive to and concerned about accuracy and detail. 'particular' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'gullible' tourist fell victim to an obvious financial scam.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'gullible' means easily persuaded to believe something. 'credulous' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'She spoke English with 'impeccable' grammar and diction.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'impeccable' means in accordance with the highest standards; faultless. 'flawless' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Through 'judicious' management of resources, the company avoided debt.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'judicious' means having, showing, or done with good judgment. 'wise' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The extreme heat made the workers feel 'lethargic' in the afternoon.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'lethargic' means affected by lethargy; sluggish and apathetic. 'sluggish' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The victor showed a 'magnanimous' gesture by praising his opponent.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'magnanimous' means generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival. 'generous' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Police uncovered a 'nefarious' plot to smuggle contraband goods.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'nefarious' means wicked or criminal in nature. 'wicked' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Despite expert advice, he remained 'obstinate' in his refusal.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'obstinate' means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion. 'stubborn' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The detective formulated a 'plausible' theory regarding the entry point.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'plausible' means seeming reasonable or probable. 'credible' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The local economy proved 'resilient' despite economic headwinds.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'resilient' means able to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions. 'durable' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Please remove all 'superfluous' details from the summary report.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'superfluous' means exceeding what is sufficient or required. 'unnecessary' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'taciturn' guard rarely uttered more than a few words.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'taciturn' means reserved or uncommunicative in speech. 'reserved' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'He offered a 'vehement' denial when accused of misconduct.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'vehement' means showing strong feeling; forceful, passionate, or intense. 'passionate' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'zealous' young activist campaigned tirelessly for environmental protection.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'zealous' means having or showing zeal; passionate. 'enthusiastic' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The doctor prescribed medication to 'alleviate' the sharp joint pain.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'alleviate' means make suffering or a problem less severe. 'relieve' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The medical scan revealed that the tumor was entirely 'benign'.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'benign' means gentle and kindly; not harmful. 'harmless' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'She presented a 'cogent' argument that persuaded the panel.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'cogent' means clear, logical, and convincing. 'compelling' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Through 'diligent' research, the historian uncovered lost documents.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'diligent' means having or showing care and conscientiousness in one's work. 'assiduous' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The lawyer delivered an 'eloquent' closing statement to the jury.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'eloquent' means fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing. 'articulate' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'It proved 'futile' to negotiate with someone who refused to listen.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'futile' means incapable of producing any useful result. 'pointless' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'garrulous' passenger talked incessantly throughout the long journey.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'garrulous' means excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters. 'talkative' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'His 'impetuous' decision to quit his job caught everyone by surprise.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'impetuous' means acting or done quickly and without thought or care. 'impulsive' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The 'loquacious' host kept the guests entertained with humorous anecdotes.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'loquacious' means tending to talk a great deal; talkative. 'talkative' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The caterpillar underwent a complete 'metamorphosis' into a butterfly.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'metamorphosis' means a change of the form or nature of a thing. 'transformation' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'He maintained a 'nonchalant' attitude despite the impending deadline.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'nonchalant' means feeling or appearing casually calm and relaxed. 'unconcerned' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The origin of the ancient manuscript remains 'obscure'.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'obscure' means not discovered or known about; uncertain. 'unclear' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'She sat by the window in a 'pensive' mood, gazing at the rain.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'pensive' means engaged in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought. 'thoughtful' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Automation rendered several traditional factory roles 'redundant'.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'redundant' means not or no longer needed or useful. 'superfluous' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Auditors were brought in to 'scrutinize' the company's account ledgers.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'scrutinize' means examine or inspect closely and thoroughly. 'examine' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'They enjoyed a 'tranquil' evening beside the calm mountain lake.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'tranquil' means free from disturbance; calm. 'peaceful' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Plastic bags have become a 'ubiquitous' source of environmental pollution.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'ubiquitous' means present, appearing, or found everywhere. 'widespread' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'New DNA evidence served to 'vindicate' the wrongly accused man.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'vindicate' means clear someone of blame or suspicion. 'exonerate' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Investors are rightfully 'wary' of putting capital into unproven ventures.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'wary' means feeling or showing caution about possible dangers. 'cautious' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Her commercial 'acumen' helped turn the small startup into a global brand.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'acumen' means the ability to make good judgments and quick decisions. 'shrewdness' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The director emphasized the need for 'brevity' in executive summaries.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'brevity' means concise and exact use of words in writing or speech. 'conciseness' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Rising costs forced the university to 'curtail' its evening programs.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'curtail' means reduce in extent or quantity; impose a restriction on. 'reduce' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Smoking exerts a 'deleterious' effect on pulmonary cardiovascular health.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'deleterious' means causing harm or damage. 'harmful' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Delaying repair work will only 'exacerbate' structural building damage.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'exacerbate' means make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse. 'worsen' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Refusing to obey the court order was a 'flagrant' breach of the law.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'flagrant' means conspicuously or obviously offensive. 'blatant' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Scientific laws describe 'immutable' patterns governing the physical universe.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'immutable' means unchanging over time or unable to be changed. 'unchangeable' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'The gallery exhibition chose to 'juxtapose' ancient pottery with modern art.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'juxtapose' means place or deal with close together for contrasting effect. 'collocate' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'His 'laconic' reply conveyed agreement without elaboration.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'laconic' means using very few words. 'brief' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Planting trees helps 'mitigate' the adverse impact of urban soil erosion.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'mitigate' means make less severe, serious, or painful. 'alleviate' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'Floppy disks have been rendered completely 'obsolete' by flash drives.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'obsolete' means no longer produced or used; out of date. 'outdated' is its nearest synonym in this context.

qs.q: 'It seems 'paradoxical' that resting can sometimes increase overall energy.' Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals.
qs.e: The word 'paradoxical' means seemingly absurd or self-contradictory. 'contradictory' is its nearest synonym in this context.
