qs.e: Monoculture encourages host-specific pest and pathogen populations while selectively depleting specific soil nutrients.

qs.q: Which traditional storage structure is constructed with elevated wooden poles and thatched roofing to dry maize cobs in West Africa?
qs.e: Maize cribs are ventilated wooden structures with wire mesh or slats that allow ambient air to dry unhusked corn cobs.

qs.q: What traditional mud-walled grain store is widely used for millet and sorghum storage in northern West Africa?
qs.e: Rhumbu is a traditional mud granary built on stone pedestals with thatched roofs, common in savanna zones.

qs.q: What is the recommended planting depth for small-seeded crops such as lettuce and tomatoes in nursery beds?
qs.e: Small seeds have minimal endosperm reserves and must be sown shallowly (0.5-1 cm) to enable emergence.

qs.q: What is the main cause of seed decay and damping-off disease in over-watered nursery beds?
o: Excessive solar radiation burning seed coats
Over-application of dry coarse wood ash
Fungal pathogens thriving in wet, poorly aerated soil
qs.e: Over-watering creates humid, anaerobic conditions favoring soil-borne damping-off fungi (Pythium, Rhizoctonia).

qs.q: What is the principal advantage of using certified seeds purchased from authorized seed companies?
o: High genetic purity, high germination percentage, and freedom from seed-borne diseases
Zero need for water or fertilizer
qs.e: Certified seed is produced under strict quality control, guaranteeing genetic purity, high germination, and disease freedom.

qs.q: What field practice involves cultivating alternating strips of erosion-resisting cover crops and clean-tilled arable crops?
qs.e: Strip cropping alternates strips of dense soil-conserving crops with erosion-prone crops across field slopes.

qs.q: Which crop pest insect belongs to the order Orthoptera and defoliates cassava plants during dry season months?
qs.e: Zonocerus variegatus (variegated grasshopper) is a major chewing pest that defoliates cassava and vegetable crops.

qs.q: Which insect vector transmits the cassava mosaic virus while feeding on plant phloem sap?
qs.e: Bemisia tabaci (whitefly) vectors cassava mosaic begomoviruses during sap feeding.

qs.q: Which non-insect field pest damages root systems of crops by forming root galls or knots?
qs.e: Meloidogyne species (root-knot nematodes) invade plant roots, forming characteristic swollen galls that disrupt water transport.

qs.q: What type of pest control uses natural predators, parasitoids, or pathogens to reduce pest populations below economic thresholds?
qs.e: Biological control utilizes natural enemies (e.g. parasitic wasps, predatory ladybird beetles) to manage pest populations.

qs.q: Which vertebrate pest attacks ripening cereal grains in large flocks across savanna regions?
qs.e: Quelea quelea (red-billed quelea bird) forms massive swarms that destroy cereal fields in semi-arid zones.

qs.q: Which pest control strategy combines biological, cultural, physical, and chemical tactics to maintain pests below damage levels?
qs.e: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) evaluates all control options holistically to keep pests below economic threshold.

qs.q: What chemical classification group includes insecticides designed to kill target insects upon physical contact with their cuticle?
qs.e: Contact insecticides penetrate the insect exoskeleton directly upon physical spraying or contact.

qs.q: Which insecticide type is absorbed by plant tissues and translocated through vascular streams to kill sap-sucking pests?
qs.e: Systemic insecticides travel through plant sap, poisoning sap-feeding pests like aphids and whiteflies.

qs.q: Which rodent species causes extensive field damage to sugarcane stems and root crops in West Africa?
qs.e: Thryonomys swinderianus (cane rat/grasscutter) gnaws on sugarcane stalks and root crops.

qs.q: Which pest control measure uses quarantine regulations to prevent introducing exotic pests into a country?
qs.e: Legislative control enforces plant quarantine laws and port inspections to exclude alien pests.

qs.q: Which cultural practice disrupts the life cycle of soil-inhabiting insect pupae by exposing them to solar heat and predators?
qs.e: Deep ploughing exposes soil-dwelling larvae, pupae, and eggs to desiccation and bird predation.

qs.q: Which fungal pathogen causes cocoa black pod disease in West Africa?
qs.e: Phytophthora palmivora (and Phytophthora megakarya) are the oomycete fungal pathogens causing cocoa black pod rot.

qs.q: Which viral disease of cocoa causes swollen stems, leaf chlorosis, and pod distortion, transmitted by mealybugs?
qs.e: Cocoa swollen shoot virus (CSSV) causes stem swelling and dieback; infected trees are rogued out.

qs.q: What symptoms indicate maize rust disease caused by Puccinia polysora?
o: Water-soaked leaf spots turning dark black
Stunted stems with yellow leaf mosaic
Reddish-brown powdery pustules on leaf surfaces
qs.e: Maize rust produces small, reddish-brown powdery urediniospores in pustules covering leaves.

qs.q: What type of pathogen causes groundnut rosette disease transmitted by aphids?
qs.e: Groundnut rosette is caused by a complex of three viral agents (GRV, GRAV, and satellite RNA) transmitted by aphids.

qs.q: Which disease of maize causes yellow and green longitudinal stripes on leaves and severe plant stunting, transmitted by leafhoppers?
qs.e: Maize streak virus (MSV) causes yellow chlorotic streaks parallel to leaf veins, transmitted by Cicadulina leafhoppers.

qs.q: What chemical fungicide group is commonly sprayed to control cocoa black pod disease?
qs.e: Copper oxide or copper hydroxide sprays protect cocoa pods against Phytophthora fungal infection.

qs.q: Which control measure is most effective for managing viral crop diseases in the field?
o: Spraying heavy doses of chemical fungicides
Applying nitrogenous fertilizer directly on leaves
Planting resistant varieties and controlling insect vectors
qs.e: Viruses cannot be cured with synthetic chemicals; control relies on vector suppression, field sanitation, and resistant crops.

qs.q: What term describes the complete destruction and removal of diseased crop plants from farmlands to prevent disease spread?
qs.e: Rogueing is the systematic uprooting and destruction of infected plants to remove pathogen inoculum sources.

qs.q: Which fungal disease causes powdery white fungal growth on upper surfaces of cucurbit and okra leaves?
qs.e: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe species) forms white powdery mycelial mats on leaf surfaces in dry, humid air.

qs.q: What term describes a sudden, widespread outbreak of a crop disease causing severe yield destruction across a region?
qs.e: An epidemic (or epiphytotic) is a rapid, widespread disease outbreak affecting large plant populations.

qs.q: Which pathogen causes root knot disease in solanaceous and leguminous crops?
qs.e: Meloidogyne nematodes invade roots and induce giant cell formation, resulting in root galls.

qs.q: Which disease symptom is characterized by localized death of plant leaf tissues, forming dark brown spots?
qs.e: Necrosis is the death of cells or tissues, appearing as brown or black dead lesions on leaves or stems.

qs.q: Which broadleaf weed species is commonly known as Siam weed and forms dense thickets in tropical fallows?
qs.e: Chromolaena odorata (Siam weed) is an aggressive invasive woody shrub that smothers crops and pastures.

qs.q: Which perennial grass weed possesses underground creeping rhizomes that make complete eradication difficult?
qs.e: Imperata cylindrica (spear grass) regenerates aggressively from sharp subterranean rhizome networks.

qs.q: Which parasitic weed species attacks roots of sorghum, maize, and millet, absorbing water and nutrients?
qs.e: Striga hermonthica (witchweed) is an obligate root parasite of cereal crops in savanna zones.

qs.q: Which weed possesses triangular stems and reproduces via underground tubers or nutlets?
qs.e: Cyperus rotundus (purple nut sedge) is a sedge with characteristic triangular stems and tubers.

qs.q: Which chemical herbicide is a non-selective, systemic compound used to clear all vegetation prior to planting?
qs.e: Glyphosate is a broad-spectrum non-selective systemic herbicide that translocates throughout plant roots and shoots.

qs.q: What term describes herbicides applied to the soil before crop seeds or weeds emerge?
qs.e: Pre-emergence herbicides are applied to soil after planting but before weed seedlings germinate.

qs.q: Which weed control method uses weed-eating insects or specific pathogens to suppress weed populations?
qs.e: Biological weed control deploys specific natural enemies (e.g., bio-herbicides, phytophagous beetles) against target weeds.

qs.q: Which weed species is commonly called bull grass or crowfoot grass and invades farmlands and footpaths?
qs.e: Eleusine indica (crowfoot grass) is a tough annual grass with digitate spikelets resistant to trampling.

qs.q: Which weed species is known as Bermuda grass or Bahama grass, forming dense creeping lawns and mats?
qs.e: Cynodon dactylon (Bermuda grass) spreads via stolons and rhizomes, acting as both pasture grass and weed.

qs.q: Which cultural weed control method involves planting dense cover crops that shade out emerging weed seedlings?
qs.e: Dense smother crops form rapid leaf canopies that intercept sunlight, inhibiting light-sensitive weed seeds.

qs.q: Which weed species produces yellow daisy-like flowers and rough hairy leaves, known as wild sunflower?
qs.e: Aspilia africana (haemorrhage plant/wild sunflower) is a common perennial composite weed.

qs.q: What term describes the accumulation of weed seeds in farmland soil over successive cropping seasons?
qs.e: The soil seed bank comprises all viable weed seeds present in soil horizons and surface litter.

qs.q: Which mechanical weed control implement is pulled behind a tractor to uproot shallow weeds between crop rows?
qs.e: Inter-row cultivators have tines or sweeps adjusted to loosen surface soil and uproot weeds between crop rows.

qs.q: What is the primary process responsible for the physical breakdown of parent rocks into smaller soil particles without altering their chemical composition?
o: Disintegration by temperature fluctuations and frost action
qs.e: Physical weathering involves mechanical disintegration caused by temperature changes, frost action, wind, and water action without altering chemical composition.

qs.q: Which soil horizon is commonly referred to as the zone of illuviation where minerals leached from topsoil accumulate?
qs.e: The B horizon (subsoil) is the illuvial horizon where clay, iron, and aluminium oxides leached from the A horizon accumulate.

qs.q: Which agricultural practice is most effective in controlling sheet erosion on gently sloping tropical farmlands?
qs.e: Contour ploughing creates ridges across slopes that slow run-off, while cover crops protect topsoil from raindrops.

qs.q: Which form of soil erosion creates deep, steep-sided channels that cannot be erased by normal tillage implements?
qs.e: Gully erosion produces wide, deep trenches that obstruct machinery and cannot be smoothed out by standard tillage.

qs.q: Which chemical compound is commonly applied to agricultural soils to reduce soil acidity and elevate soil pH?
qs.e: Calcium carbonate (agricultural lime) neutralizes excess hydrogen ions in acid soils, thereby raising pH.

qs.q: Which soil organism converts atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonium ions in mutualistic association with leguminous roots?
qs.e: Rhizobium bacteria form root nodules on legumes and fix atmospheric nitrogen into plant-usable nitrogenous compounds.

qs.q: What soil structure type is considered most desirable for arable crop cultivation due to optimal aeration and water retention?
qs.e: Crumb structure consists of porous, spherical aggregates that provide an optimal balance of aeration, drainage, and moisture retention.

qs.q: Which process of chemical weathering involves the addition of oxygen to minerals containing iron compounds?
qs.e: Oxidation occurs when mineral elements (like ferrous iron) react with oxygen to form oxides, weakening the rock structure.

qs.q: Which physical process causes soil water to move upward against gravity through narrow pore channels?
qs.e: Capillarity occurs due to surface tension and adhesion of water molecules to soil particle surfaces in small pores.

qs.q: Which component of soil organic matter represents the dark, stable, colloidal material resulting from advanced decomposition?
qs.e: Humus is the complex, dark brown, highly resistant organic residue that improves nutrient retention and soil structure.

qs.q: Which mechanical soil conservation structure consists of a bank and channel constructed across a slope to intercept run-off?
qs.e: Terraces are step-like structures built across steep slopes to reduce runoff velocity and retain soil moisture.

qs.q: Which condition leads to oxygen deficiency in soil pore spaces and adversely affects root respiration?
qs.e: Waterlogging saturates pore spaces with water, displacing soil air and leading to anaerobic conditions.

qs.q: Which type of water erosion occurs when thin layers of topsoil are uniformly removed across a broad field surface?
qs.e: Sheet erosion involves the uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil over a wide area by overland water flow.

qs.q: What is the primary function of earthworms in improving soil fertility?
o: Fixing atmospheric nitrogen directly into soil pores
Excreting synthetic pesticides that kill weed seeds
Converting sand grains into clay minerals
Incorporating organic matter and forming fertile casts rich in nutrients
qs.e: Earthworms ingest organic material and soil, depositing nutrient-rich casts that enhance soil structure and fertility.

qs.q: Which macro-nutrient is essential for chlorophyll synthesis and constitutes the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule?
qs.e: Magnesium is the central metallic ion in the chlorophyll molecule, making it indispensable for photosynthesis.

qs.q: What typical visual symptom indicates nitrogen deficiency in cereal crops such as maize?
o: Purpling along the margins of young leaves
V-shaped chlorosis starting at the tip of older leaves
qs.e: Nitrogen is mobile in plants; deficiency causes yellowing (chlorosis) that starts at the tips of older lower leaves in a V-pattern.

qs.q: Which plant nutrient deficiency manifests as purpling or reddening of leaves and delayed crop maturity?
qs.e: Phosphorus deficiency restricts cell division and leads to anthocyanin accumulation, causing purple discoloration.

qs.q: Which practice involves ploughing under young green leguminous crops to enrich the soil with organic matter and nitrogen?
qs.e: Green manuring is the practice of growing leguminous crops (e.g. Mucuna, Crotalaria) and incorporate them into soil while green.

qs.q: What is the primary role of potassium in plant physiological processes?
o: Regulation of stomatal opening and water balance
Component of nucleic acids and ATP
qs.e: Potassium acts as an osmotic regulator, controlling stomatal guard cell movement, enzyme activation, and water relations.

qs.q: Which inorganic fertilizer supplies both nitrogen and sulphur to agricultural crops?
qs.e: Ammonium sulphate [(NH4)2SO4] provides 21% nitrogen and 24% sulphur.

qs.q: Which practice accelerates the breakdown of organic materials in compost heaps by maintaining moisture and turning?
o: Compacting compost tightly to exclude air
Aeration and moistening of compost layers
Keeping compost totally dry at all times
qs.e: Aerobic decomposition requires adequate oxygen (provided by turning) and moisture (around 50-60%) for microbial activity.

qs.q: What chemical compound in agricultural lime neutralizes excess hydrogen ions in acid soils?
qs.e: Calcium carbonate reacts with H+ ions in soil solution to form water and carbon dioxide, raising soil pH.

qs.q: Which fertilizer application method involves placing fertilizer in concentrated bands beside crop rows?
qs.e: Side dressing places fertilizer in bands along the side of growing crop rows for efficient root uptake.

qs.q: Which deficiency symptom is typical of potassium lack in matured cassava leaves?
o: Uniform pale yellowing of entire plant
Marginal scorching and brown necrosis of leaf margins
qs.e: Potassium deficiency causes leaf margins to dry out and turn brown, appearing scorched or burnt.

qs.q: Which agricultural crop is commonly planted as a green manure crop in tropical West Africa?
qs.e: Mucuna pruriens (velvet bean) is a leguminous cover crop widely grown to restore soil fertility and suppress weeds.

qs.q: Which practice minimizes nutrient leaching in coarse-textured sandy soils under high rainfall conditions?
o: Applying all fertilizer in one massive pre-plant dosage
Tilling soil deeply during heavy rainfall
qs.e: Dividing total fertilizer into multiple smaller applications matches crop uptake and minimizes leaching losses.

qs.q: Which form of soil water is held between field capacity and permanent wilting point and is readily absorbed by crop roots?
qs.e: Capillary water held in medium soil pores between field capacity (-0.3 bar) and wilting point (-15 bar) is accessible to roots.

qs.q: What condition occurs when soil moisture drops to a point where plants wilt permanently and cannot recover even when placed in a humid environment?
qs.e: At permanent wilting point (suction of ~15 atmospheres), soil holds water so tightly that roots cannot extract it, leading to irreversible wilting.

qs.q: What term describes the combined loss of water from soil surface evaporation and plant transpiration?
qs.e: Evapotranspiration (ET) represents total water loss to the atmosphere through evaporation from soil/vegetation and transpiration from plants.

qs.q: What is the primary objective of constructing subsurface tile drains in waterlogged agricultural fields?
o: Raise soil temperature above 50 degrees Celsius
Lower the water table and improve root zone aeration
qs.e: Subsurface drainage removes excess gravitational water from the root zone, lowering the water table and restoring aeration.

qs.q: What parameter defines the maximum water content a soil can retain after excess gravitational water has drained away?
qs.e: Field capacity is the amount of water remaining in soil 2-3 days after heavy rainfall or irrigation when gravitational drainage stops.

qs.q: Which surface irrigation method involves running water down narrow parallel channels created between crop rows?
qs.e: In furrow irrigation, water flows down small channels (furrows) between crop ridges, seeping laterally into crop root zones.

qs.q: What happens to crop root respiration when soil becomes completely saturated and waterlogged for extended periods?
o: Respiration increases dramatically due to excess hydrogen
Root cells start producing high glucose levels
Respiration rate drops sharply due to lack of dissolved oxygen
Stomata open fully to release excess nitrogen
qs.e: Waterlogging displaces soil air, causing anaerobic conditions that inhibit aerobic root respiration and ATP production.

qs.q: What term describes the downward movement of water through the soil profile past the root zone?
qs.e: Percolation is the movement of water downward through soil layers under gravity.

qs.q: What is the main benefit of installing drip irrigation in arid fruit orchards?
o: Maximizes water use efficiency by minimizing evaporation
Cools air temperature around tree canopy
Washes insect pests directly off tree leaves
Increases soil erosion around tree roots
qs.e: Drip irrigation targets water directly to root zones, achieving water efficiency exceeding 90% by limiting surface evaporation.

qs.q: Which factor increases the rate of plant transpiration under field crop conditions?
o: High atmospheric humidity and low temperature
High wind velocity and high temperature
Calm wind conditions and low solar radiation
qs.e: High temperatures and wind remove water vapour from around leaf surfaces, increasing the vapor pressure gradient and transpiration rate.

qs.q: Which tractor component transmits rotational mechanical power directly to stationary or trailed implements like sprayers and mowers?
qs.e: The Power Take-Off (PTO) shaft transmits tractor engine torque to power driven implements.

qs.q: Which system attaches heavy mounted implements to the rear of a tractor using two lower draft links and one top link?
qs.e: The three-point linkage attaches mounted implements, allowing hydraulic height and draft control.

qs.q: Which tillage implement is designed to break up deep impervious hardpans without turning over topsoil?
qs.e: Subsoilers feature long heavy shanks that penetrate deep (40-60 cm) to shatter hardpans without inversion.

qs.q: Which heavy hand tool combines a axe blade and a pick head used for uprooting tree stumps and breaking hard ground?
qs.e: A mattock features a horizontal adze blade and vertical axe blade for chopping roots and stumping.

qs.q: Which machine implement uses L-shaped rotating blades driven by PTO shaft to pulverize soil into a fine seedbed?
qs.e: Rotovators feature power-driven rotating tines that mix and pulverize soil in a single pass.

qs.q: Which component of a disc plough scrapes off sticky soil from the rotating concave disc face during operation?
qs.e: Disc scrapers sit against inner disc curves to scrape away adhering sticky clay.

qs.q: Which planting implement opens seed furrows, drops seeds at uniform intervals, covers them, and presses soil in one pass?
qs.e: Seed drills meter seeds through tubes into open furrows, covering and rolling them automatically.

qs.q: What component in a knapsack sprayer pressurizes liquid chemical in the spray tank during manual pumping?
qs.e: Manual lever pumping operates a internal piston/diaphragm pump that pressurizes liquid in the air chamber.

qs.q: What device in a tractor engine air intake system filters out dust and abrasive particles before air enters combustion cylinders?
qs.e: Air cleaners (dry paper or oil-bath types) strip dust particles from incoming air to prevent cylinder wall scoring.

qs.q: Which tractor component transfers engine power to drive wheels through a variable gear selection system?
qs.e: The transmission gearbox provides speed and torque ratio changes to adapt tractor output to field loads.

qs.q: Which implement is specially constructed with a cylindrical roller to compact loose soil over seeds?
qs.e: Land rollers crush surface clods and press loose soil tightly around seeds to facilitate water absorption.

qs.q: Which engine cooling system component circulates liquid coolant through engine water jackets and radiator core?
qs.e: The centrifugal water pump circulates coolant through engine blocks to transfer heat to radiator fins.

qs.q: Which farm implement uses rigid or spring tines to loosen topsoil and pull weeds between crop rows?
qs.e: Cultivators use narrow tines or sweeps to break surface crusts and uproot weeds between growing rows.

qs.q: Which harvesting machine cuts standing cereal stalks and lays them neatly in swaths on the ground?
qs.e: Reapers cut standing cereal crops mechanically, laying stalks in windrows for manual gathering.

qs.q: Which machine compresses cured hay or straw into rectangular or cylindrical dense bundles tied with twine?
qs.e: Balers pick up field windrows and compress forage into tight, transportable bales bound with twine or wire.

qs.q: Which tractor hitch component provides a single pivot point for towing trailing implements like trailers?
qs.e: The swinging drawbar provides a heavy tow point for trailed implements and farm wagons.

qs.q: What tool is used to bore deep vertical holes in ground soil for erecting fence posts?
qs.e: Post hole augers (manual or tractor PTO-driven helical screws) excavate neat cylindrical post holes.

qs.q: How many total links are present in a standard Gunter's surveying chain measuring 66 feet in total length?
qs.e: A Gunter's chain is 66 feet (20.12 m) long and divided into exactly 100 equal links (each link = 0.66 ft).

qs.q: Which surveying instrument uses a magnetic needle and a sighting prism to measure magnetic bearings of survey lines?
qs.e: Prismatic compasses determine magnetic bearings of survey lines relative to magnetic North.

qs.q: Which optical surveying instrument is mounted on a tripod and used to measure height differences and establish horizontal elevation planes?
qs.e: Dumpy levels establish horizontal line-of-sight planes to read leveling staves for elevation determination.

qs.q: Which surveying tool consists of small steel wire pins with ring tops used to mark chain lengths along a line?
qs.e: Arrows (steel marking pins) are inserted into ground at each chain length count.

qs.q: What term describes lateral perpendicular measurements taken from a main survey chain line to boundary features?
qs.e: Offsets are perpendicular distances measured left or right from a main baseline to locate field details.

qs.q: Which line forms the principal long framework line running through the center of a farm survey area?
qs.e: The baseline is the longest main survey line from which secondary framework lines and offsets originate.

qs.q: Which weighted cone-shaped tool suspended on a string establishes true vertical lines during surveying and construction?
qs.e: A plumb bob uses gravity to center surveying instruments precisely over ground station marks.

qs.q: What field tool is a 3-metre wooden rod marked in graduations held vertically for reading height through a dumpy level?
qs.e: A leveling staff (or rod) is a graduated staff read through telescope crosshairs to measure elevation differences.

qs.q: What calculation converts a land area of 45,000 square metres into hectares?
qs.e: 1 hectare = 10,000 square metres. Area in hectares = 45,000 m² / 10,000 = 4.5 ha.

qs.q: Which map feature represents lines joining points of equal elevation above sea level on topographic maps?
qs.e: Contour lines connect terrain points sharing identical elevation above mean sea level.

qs.q: What is indicated on a topographic map when contour lines are drawn very close together?
qs.e: Closely spaced contour lines indicate a rapid elevation change over short horizontal distance (steep slope).

qs.q: What term describes the systematic measurement and mapping of land elevation contours for farm drainage planning?
qs.e: Topographic surveys map elevation contours, watercourses, and physical surface features.

qs.q: What preliminary survey phase involves walking over a farm site to inspect terrain features before setting baseline stations?
qs.e: Reconnaissance is the initial visual field inspection to assess site layout and select suitable survey stations.

qs.q: Which chemical group kills subterranean parasitic root-knot roundworms?
qs.e: Nematicides eliminate parasitic soil nematodes that infect plant root systems.

qs.q: Which direction relative to wind movement should an operator walk while spraying chemical pesticides?
o: Downwind with wind blowing behind or across operator
qs.e: Spraying downwind carries chemical mist swaths away from the operator's body and face.

qs.q: What term describes the required waiting period between chemical pesticide application and crop harvest for safe consumption?
qs.e: Pre-harvest interval (PHI) is the mandatory delay between chemical application and harvest to allow toxic residues to degrade.

qs.q: Which chemical formulation code 'EC' printed on agrochemical containers stands for?
qs.e: Emulsifiable Concentrate (EC) contains active ingredient dissolved in oil solvent with emulsifiers that mix with water.

qs.q: Which agrochemical formulation code 'WP' designates finely ground dry chemical powder mixed with water?
qs.e: Wettable Powder (WP) consists of fine dry particles suspended in water with wetting agents.

qs.q: Which organochlorine insecticide was banned globally due to high environmental persistence and bioaccumulation in food chains?
qs.e: DDT (Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) is a persistent organochlorine that bioaccumulates in fatty tissues.

qs.q: Which class of synthetic insecticides is derived from natural pyrethrin compounds found in Chrysanthemum flowers?
qs.e: Synthetic pyrethroids (e.g. permethrin, cypermethrin) mimic natural pyrethrins, offering fast knockdown and low mammalian toxicity.

qs.q: What term defines the process of measuring actual liquid delivery rate of a sprayer per unit field area before spraying?
qs.e: Calibration determines liquid volume delivered per hectare, ensuring correct chemical dosage.

qs.q: What color safety band printed on agrochemical container labels designates extremely hazardous toxic chemicals?
qs.e: Red hazard bands denote WHO Class Ia/Ib extremely and highly hazardous pesticides.

qs.q: What color safety band on agrochemical labels indicates caution and lower toxicity hazards?
qs.e: Green hazard bands denote WHO Class III slightly hazardous or unlikely toxic products.

qs.q: What term describes movement of sprayed pesticide droplets off-target away from intended crop fields during windy weather?
qs.e: Spray drift occurs when wind currents carry fine spray droplets away from target fields during application.

qs.q: What physical soil property is most critical when selecting a site for constructing earthen fish ponds?
o: Coarse sandy texture with high permeability
High peat content with acid pH 3.0
High clay content of 20 to 30 percent to retain water
qs.e: Clay soil prevents seepage water losses, ensuring earthen pond dikes retain water.

qs.q: Which structure controls water release from earthen fish ponds during drainage and harvesting operations?
qs.e: A monk is a concrete drainage structure with flashboards and screens used to regulate water depth and drain ponds completely.

qs.q: What is the primary function of an emergency spillway in earthen pond dam construction?
o: Filtering fine plankton out of incoming water
Discharging excess flood water safely to prevent dam wall collapse
Providing shallow spawning beds for fingerlings
Trapping predatory wild fish entering the pond
qs.e: Spillways allow heavy flood runoff to bypass pond dikes safely, preventing dam breach.

qs.q: Why is agricultural lime applied to fish pond bottoms prior to stocking fingerlings?
o: Kills all beneficial green algae permanently
Reduces water dissolved oxygen levels to zero
Neutralizes soil acidity, raises total alkalinity, and clears turbid water
Turns pond water into saline ocean water
qs.e: Liming neutralizes acidic pond muds, buffers pH fluctuations, and releases phosphorus for phytoplankton growth.

qs.q: What term describes microscopic microscopic floating photosynthetic plant organisms in aquatic pond ecosystems?
qs.e: Phytoplankton are microscopic algae that generate oxygen and serve as primary producers in fish ponds.

qs.q: What term describes microscopic floating animal organisms such as rotifers and daphnia in fish ponds?
qs.e: Zooplankton are tiny aquatic animals feeding on phytoplankton, serving as live food for fish fry.

qs.q: Which fishing gear consists of a long net wall dragged through shallow water by two teams to surround fish?
qs.e: Beach seines are long netting walls pulled through water toward shore to encircle fish.

qs.q: What fish preservation method uses high sodium chloride concentrations to draw out moisture by osmosis?
qs.e: Salting creates high osmotic pressure, dehydrating fish cells and suppressing bacterial growth.

qs.q: Which simple device consisting of a black and white patterned disc is lowered into pond water to measure turbidity?
qs.e: A Secchi disc measures water clarity and plankton density by recording the depth where the disc disappears.

qs.q: What term describes stripping eggs from female catfish and mixing them with milt stripped from male testes in hatcheries?
qs.e: Stripping manually expresses ripe eggs into dry bowls, fertilized by adding stripped male semen (milt).

qs.q: What aquaculture system raises fish inside floating mesh net enclosures suspended in lakes or reservoirs?
qs.e: Cage culture holds fish in submerged net cages suspended from floating collar frames in large water bodies.

qs.q: What is the primary function of mechanical paddlewheel aerators installed in intensive fish ponds?
o: Filtering floating duckweed out of water
Raising pond water temperature above 45 degrees
Dissolving atmospheric oxygen into pond water and degassing carbon dioxide
qs.e: Paddlewheel aerators splash pond surface water, increasing atmospheric oxygen transfer and degassing harmful gases.

qs.q: What hybrid catfish produced by crossing Clarias gariepinus and Heterobranchus longifilis is prized in Nigerian aquaculture?
qs.e: Heteroclarias is an intergeneric hybrid combining rapid growth and disease resistance.

qs.q: What term defines rearing two or more compatible fish species with different feeding habits together in the same pond?
qs.e: Polyculture (e.g., combining surface-feeding Tilapia and bottom-feeding Catfish) maximizes natural food web utilization.

qs.q: What practice combines fish culture with crop or livestock production, such as pig-cum-fish farming?
qs.e: Integrated farming uses animal manure directly to fertilize fish ponds, optimizing resource recycling.

qs.q: What term describes the natural process where nutrient enrichment leads to excessive algal growth in aquatic bodies?
qs.e: Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment (N and P) causing dense algal blooms that deplete oxygen upon decay.

qs.q: Which active fishing gear uses a large cone-shaped net dragged along the seabed behind a motorized vessel?
qs.e: Trawl nets are funnel-shaped nets towed along seabed bottoms by trawlers to capture demersal fish and shrimp.

qs.q: Which economic timber tree indigenous to West African rainforests is botanically named Milicia excelsa?
qs.e: Milicia excelsa (formerly Chlorophora excelsa) is the botanical name for Iroko, a premier hardwood timber.

qs.q: Which West African timber tree species produces dark reddish-brown hardwood widely exported for luxury furniture?
qs.e: Khaya ivorensis (African mahogany) yields durable reddish timber prized for cabinet making.

qs.q: Which fast-growing softwood tree species is widely planted in West African forest plantations for paper pulp production?
qs.e: Gmelina arborea is a fast-growing exotic tree cultivated extensively for pulpwood and matchsticks.

qs.q: Which forest management practice integrates the cultivation of arable food crops alongside young forest tree seedlings?
qs.e: The Taungya system allows farmers to grow arable crops between young plantation trees until tree canopies close.

qs.q: Which exotic hardwood timber tree species imported from Asia is botanically named Tectona grandis?
qs.e: Tectona grandis (Teak) produces durable, weather-resistant hardwood rich in natural oils.

qs.q: What branch of forestry deals with the establishment, cultivation, and care of forest trees?
qs.e: Silviculture is the science and practice of controlling forest establishment, composition, structure, and growth.

qs.q: Which non-timber forest product harvested from Acacia senegal trees in dry savannas is used as a commercial emulsifier?
qs.e: Gum arabic is a natural exudate harvested from Acacia senegal used in food, pharmaceuticals, and soft drinks.

qs.q: Which forest harvesting practice selects and fells only mature trees exceeding minimum girth limits?
qs.e: Selective exploitation cuts individual trees above specified diameter limits, leaving younger trees to mature.

qs.q: What forestry practice removes overcrowded or malformed young trees from a stand to accelerate growth of crop trees?
qs.e: Thinning reduces tree density in young forest stands, concentrating light and nutrients on superior timber trees.

qs.q: Which forest ecosystem along coastal tropical estuaries is dominated by stilt-rooted Rhizophora species?
qs.e: Mangrove forests comprise salt-tolerant Rhizophora species along tidal intertidal estuaries.

qs.q: Which afforestation project plants dense tree belts across northern borders to halt Sahara desert encroachment?
qs.e: The Great Green Wall initiative plants contiguous tree belts across Africa to combat desertification.

qs.q: What term describes establishing rows of trees planted perpendicular to prevailing winds to protect crops from wind erosion?
qs.e: Shelterbelts are linear tree plantings that reduce wind velocity, protecting topsoil and reducing crop evapotranspiration.

qs.q: Which indigenous climbing vegetable crop produces large ribbed fruits and nutrient-rich edible leaves named Telfairia occidentalis?
qs.e: Telfairia occidentalis (fluted pumpkin/ugu) is a dioecious climbing cucurbit prized for leaves and oilseeds.

qs.q: Which perennial shrub vegetable is botanically named Vernonia amygdalina and contains bitter sesquiterpene lactones?
qs.e: Vernonia amygdalina (bitter leaf) is a popular culinary and medicinal shrub vegetable.

qs.q: Which ornamental garden shrub produces showy red flowers and is botanically named Hibiscus rosa-sinensis?
qs.e: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis is a popular tropical ornamental flowering shrub.

qs.q: Which thorny ornamental climbing plant produces bright magenta paper-like bracts surrounding tiny flowers?
qs.e: Bougainvillea spectabilis is a woody thorny vine grown for colorful showy floral bracts.

qs.q: What term describes designing outdoor garden spaces using plants, lawns, rocks, and water features?
qs.e: Landscape architecture arranges living plants and hardscape features for functional aesthetic environments.

qs.q: Which nursery practice involves removing lower leaves and shoots of fruit trees to establish a strong central leader?
qs.e: Training shapes tree growth architecture during early development for optimal canopy light interception.

qs.q: Which fruit vegetable produces pungent pods containing capsaicin botanically named Capsicum frutescens?
qs.e: Capsicum frutescens (bird eye chili) contains capsaicin alkaloid that imparts pungent heat.

qs.q: Which fruit tree species produces round green fruits containing pink seed pulp rich in Vitamin C, named Psidium guajava?
qs.e: Psidium guajava (guava) fruits contain exceptional concentrations of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

qs.q: Which vegetable species is known as waterleaf and is widely cultivated in humid West Africa as a soup green?
qs.e: Talinum triangulare (waterleaf) is a succulent, fast-growing leafy vegetable.

qs.q: What term describes enclosed glass or plastic structures used to cultivate off-season horticultural crops in controlled environments?
qs.e: Greenhouses provide controlled environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, light) for year-round crop production.

qs.q: Which aromatic herb species is known as scent leaf or African basil in Nigerian cooking?
qs.e: Ocimum gratissimum (scent leaf/effirin) contains aromatic essential oils (eugenol) used in cooking and medicine.

qs.q: What tool is used by beekeepers to pry apart hive frames stuck together with propolis?
qs.e: A hive tool is a flat steel lever used to scrape propolis and separate hive bodies.

qs.q: What sticky resinous substance is collected by honeybees from tree buds to seal hive cracks and sanitize walls?
qs.e: Propolis is a resinous tree mixture with antibacterial properties used to seal hive gaps.

qs.q: What natural secretion is produced by worker bee head glands to feed young larvae and the queen bee?
qs.e: Royal jelly is a nutrient-rich glandular secretion fed to all young larvae and continuously to the queen.

qs.q: What substance is secreted by abdominal wax glands of worker bees to construct hexagonal comb cells?
qs.e: Worker bees exude liquid beeswax from abdominal glands, molding it into hexagonal comb cells.

qs.q: What term describes a portion of a honeybee colony leaving the parent hive with the old queen to establish a new nest?
qs.e: Swarming is natural colony reproduction where a queen and half the workers leave to form a new colony.

qs.q: Which modern beehive design features moveable horizontal top bars that allow honey harvesting without destroying combs?
o: Kenya Top Bar Hive or Langstroth hive
qs.e: Top bar and Langstroth hives utilize removable frames/bars that allow non-destructive honey extraction.

qs.q: Which centrifugal machine spins uncapped honeycombs to extract liquid honey without breaking wax structures?
qs.e: Honey extractors spin uncapped frames, slinging liquid honey outward while preserving wax combs.

qs.q: What term describes organisms whose genetic material has been altered using recombinant DNA technology?
qs.e: Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) carry foreign genes inserted via genetic engineering.

qs.q: What term describes propagating large quantities of disease-free plant clones from small explants in sterile tissue culture?
qs.e: Micropropagation mass-produces uniform clonal plantlets in sterile tissue culture media.

qs.q: What calculation determines the Gross Margin of a poultry enterprise that generated ₦1,200,000 in total revenue and incurred ₦700,000 in total variable costs?
qs.e: Gross Margin = Total Revenue - Total Variable Costs = ₦1,200,000 - ₦700,000 = ₦500,000.

qs.q: If a farm enterprise achieves a Gross Margin of ₦600,000 and has Total Fixed Costs of ₦200,000, what is its Net Profit?
qs.e: Net Profit = Gross Margin - Total Fixed Costs = ₦600,000 - ₦200,000 = ₦400,000.

qs.q: Which economic principle states that as additional units of a variable input are added to fixed inputs, marginal output eventually decreases?
qs.e: The Law of Diminishing Returns states that adding sequential variable inputs to fixed inputs beyond a point reduces marginal output.

qs.q: Which farm record contains a detailed list of all farm assets, physical quantities, and financial valuations at a specific date?
qs.e: An inventory record lists all physical assets (machinery, stock, supplies) and their monetary values on a given date.

qs.q: Which financial accounting statement summarizes all income and expenditure over a accounting period to reveal overall business performance?
qs.e: A Profit and Loss Account aggregates revenues earned and operating expenses incurred to calculate net profit or loss.

qs.q: Which financial statement shows the net worth of a farm business at a specific date using the formula Assets equals Liabilities plus Owner Equity?
qs.e: A Balance Sheet lists total assets, total liabilities, and net worth (equity) at a specific point in time.

qs.q: Which land tenure system in West Africa involves ownership where land is inherited collectively by family members?
qs.e: Communal/inheritance tenure allocates land rights through family bloodlines and customary community authority.

qs.q: What is a major economic disadvantage of communal land tenure fragmentation in West Africa?
o: Leads to small scattered field plots that hinder farm mechanization
qs.e: Fragmented small plots under communal inheritance hinder large-scale tractor mechanization and commercial credit access.

qs.q: Which land tenure system grants absolute private ownership and perpetual rights to buy, sell, or mortgage land?
qs.e: Freehold grants complete private title ownership, allowing unrestricted land transfer and mortgage collateral.

qs.q: Which land tenure arrangement involves a tenant farmer paying a fixed annual rent or sharing a percentage of harvested crops with the landowner?
qs.e: Leasehold or sharecropping gives temporary land use rights in exchange for cash rent or crop yield shares.

qs.q: Which parameter measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded of a farm product to changes in its price?
qs.e: Price Elasticity of Demand = Percentage change in quantity demanded / Percentage change in price.

qs.q: What happens to the supply curve of an agricultural product when a major technological breakthrough reduces production costs?
qs.e: Cost-reducing technology lowers marginal production costs, shifting the supply curve rightward (increasing supply at all prices).

qs.q: What market structure exists when a single seller controls the entire supply of an essential agricultural input like fertilizer?
qs.e: A monopoly exists when a single seller controls the entire supply of a good or service.

qs.q: Which budgeting statement outlines projected cash inflows and outflows month by month to ensure enterprise liquidity?
qs.e: Cash flow budgets project monthly timing of receipts and expenses to identify short-term borrowing needs.

qs.q: What term describes the additional revenue generated by selling one extra unit of farm output?
qs.e: Marginal Revenue (MR) = Change in Total Revenue / Change in Output Quantity.

qs.q: What term describes the additional cost incurred by producing one extra unit of crop or livestock output?
qs.e: Marginal Cost (MC) = Change in Total Cost / Change in Output Quantity.

qs.q: What form of agricultural credit is extended by agro-dealers supplying inputs to farmers with payment deferred until harvest?
qs.e: Trade credit allows farmers to receive seeds/fertilizer on credit, repaying after crop sales.

qs.q: What specialized agricultural credit institution was established by the Nigerian government to provide low-interest loans to farmers?
o: Nigerian Agricultural, Cooperative and Rural Development Bank
qs.e: NACRDB (now Bank of Agriculture, BOA) provides agricultural credit to Nigerian farmers.

qs.q: What term describes a written business plan estimating projected costs, revenues, and net profits for a proposed farm project?
qs.e: A farm budget or feasibility plan projects financial costs, expected returns, and cash flows for enterprise appraisal.

qs.q: What calculation determines the Net Worth of a farmer who owns total assets valued at ₦10,000,000 and owes total liabilities of ₦3,500,000?
qs.e: Net Worth (Owner Equity) = Total Assets - Total Liabilities = ₦10,000,000 - ₦3,500,000 = ₦6,500,000.

qs.q: Which international trade policy places import taxes on foreign agricultural imports to protect domestic farmers?
qs.e: Import tariffs add custom duties to imported produce, making domestic crops more price-competitive.

qs.q: Which trade restriction imposes a quantitative limit on the physical volume of a farm commodity imported into a country?
qs.e: Import quotas set physical limits on imported goods to prevent domestic market flooding.

qs.q: What economic concept describes the extra satisfaction or utility a consumer derives from consuming one additional unit of a crop?
qs.e: Marginal Utility (MU) measures the change in total consumer satisfaction from consuming one extra unit.

qs.q: Which economic law states that as a consumer consumes successive units of a food item, the extra satisfaction gained from each additional unit declines?
qs.e: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that additional consumption of a good yields decreasing incremental satisfaction.

qs.q: Which group extension method shows farmers step-by-step HOW to perform a new practical skill, such as operating a knapsack sprayer?
qs.e: Method demonstrations teach practical physical skills by showing step-by-step execution (showing HOW).

qs.q: Which group extension method compares the yield RESULTS of a new crop variety side-by-side with a traditional local variety over a full season?
qs.e: Result demonstrations convince farmers by showing performance comparison RESULTS over time (showing WHY).

qs.q: What is the correct sequential order of stages in the classical Innovation-Adoption Process model?
qs.e: The AIETA adoption model sequence is: Awareness -> Interest -> Evaluation -> Trial -> Adoption.

qs.q: In Rogers' adopter categorization, what term describes the small first group of farmers (2.5 percent) who risk trying new unproven technologies?
qs.e: Innovators are venturesome risk-takers (2.5%) who lead initial technology adoption.

qs.q: Which adopter category consists of respected local opinion leaders (13.5 percent) whose adoption decisions influence other community members?
qs.e: Early adopters (13.5%) are respected local opinion leaders whose approval validates new technologies for others.

qs.q: Which adopter group represents the last 16 percent of traditional farmers who resist change and adopt technologies only when forced by necessity?
qs.e: Laggards (16%) are traditionalists oriented toward past practices, highly skeptical of innovations.

qs.q: What extension system in Nigeria deployed subject matter specialists to train village extension agents on fixed bi-weekly schedules?
qs.e: The Training and Visit (T&V) system utilized strict schedules of regular training for agents and fixed farm visit cycles.

qs.q: What public agency leads agricultural extension delivery across states in Nigeria under Ministry of Agriculture supervision?
qs.e: Agricultural Development Programmes (ADPs) execute public extension services in Nigerian states.

qs.q: What extension technique trains selected progressive farmers to act as peer educators who pass technologies to neighbor farmers?
o: Contact farmer or farmer-to-farmer extension approach
qs.e: The contact farmer approach uses trained community peers to disseminate information laterally within villages.

qs.q: What extension principle emphasizes that extension programs must start from the existing needs and felt problems of rural farmers?
qs.e: Successful extension must address 'felt needs' identified by farmers themselves rather than imposed external agendas.

qs.q: Why is two-way communication essential in effective agricultural extension programs?
o: Enables agents to force farmers to adopt technologies
Guarantees government grants to extension workers
Allows farmers to feed field problems back to researchers while receiving technical solutions
Eliminates the need for field visits
qs.e: Two-way communication ensures field problems inform research priorities while research solutions flow to farmers.

qs.q: Which innovation attribute describes how easy or difficult a new technology is to understand and execute by smallholders?
qs.e: Complexity measures the degree to which an innovation is perceived as difficult to understand and implement.

qs.q: Which innovation attribute describes the degree to which an improved practice is perceived as superior to existing traditional practices?
qs.e: Relative advantage measures economic or social superiority of an innovation over traditional methods.

qs.q: Which innovation attribute describes how consistent a new technology is with existing cultural values, past experiences, and farmer needs?
qs.e: Compatibility reflects alignment with existing socio-cultural norms, values, and farming systems.

qs.q: Which innovation attribute describes the degree to which an innovation can be tested on a small scale before full adoption?
qs.e: Trialability allows farmers to experiment with innovations on small plots to reduce risk before full-scale adoption.

qs.q: Which innovation attribute describes how visible the positive results of a new technology are to neighboring community farmers?
qs.e: Observability measures how easily community peers can see physical evidence of an innovation's success.

qs.q: What field worker level in the ADP system maintains direct day-to-day contact with village farming households?
o: Village Extension Agent or Block Extension Supervisor
qs.e: Village Extension Agents (VEAs) live in rural communities, conducting direct farm visits and group meetings.

qs.q: What extension approach focuses extension resources exclusively on a single high-value export crop like cocoa or cotton?
qs.e: Commodity-specialized extension focuses all technical assistance, inputs, and marketing on one high-value cash crop.

qs.q: What term describes the ratio of extension agents to farming households in a target region?
qs.e: Agent-to-farmer ratio measures extension coverage capacity (e.g. 1 agent to 2,000 farmers in developing nations).

qs.q: How does a high extension agent-to-farmer ratio (e.g., 1 agent to 3,000 farmers) affect extension service quality?
o: Guarantees daily personal visits to every farmer
Eliminates the need for group demonstrations
Severely restricts individual farm contact and reduces service effectiveness
qs.e: Overburdened agents cannot maintain frequent personal contact, diluting extension impact across scattered populations.

qs.q: What modern digital technology uses mobile phone SMS, voice calls, and smartphone apps to deliver agricultural advice to rural farmers?
qs.e: E-extension leverages mobile phones, SMS platforms, and apps to deliver real-time advisory services directly to farmers.

qs.q: What extension teaching method brings farmers to research institutes during open-house exhibitions to view field trials?
qs.e: Field Days host community farmers at research stations or model farms to showcase multi-crop trials and machinery.

qs.q: What extension evaluation metric measures the percentage of targeted farmers who continuously practice an recommended innovation?
qs.e: Adoption rate quantifies the proportion of target population sustaining practice of a recommended innovation.

qs.q: What socio-cultural factor can severely hinder male extension agents from reaching female farmers in conservative traditional societies?
o: Total lack of female farmers in West Africa
Prohibition of agriculture by female religious leaders
Lower physical stamina of female farmers
Cultural gender restrictions prohibiting male agents from interacting directly with women
qs.e: Socio-cultural norms in conservative areas restrict male agents from visiting female farmers directly, necessitating female extension agents.

qs.q: Why is recruiting and deploying female extension agents critical in West African extension strategy?
o: Ensures direct extension access for women farmers who produce a large proportion of food crops
Reduces extension operating costs by 90 percent
Eliminates the need for transport vehicles
qs.e: Women manage significant agricultural enterprises; female agents overcome cultural barriers to deliver advisory services directly.

qs.q: What non-governmental organization approach delivers extension advice bundled with micro-credit loans and input supplies?
qs.e: Integrated NGO models package technical training alongside credit, seed supplies, and market access.

qs.q: What extension technique uses village video screenings showing model farmers demonstrating improved techniques?
qs.e: Participatory video uses locally produced video recordings of peer model farmers to trigger group discussion and adoption.

qs.q: What principles guide non-formal adult education in agricultural extension?
o: Rote memorization, military discipline, and fixed grading
Abstract mathematics, indoor lectures, and enforced attendance
Problem-centered, practical, voluntary, and building on learner experience
qs.e: Adult extension learning is non-formal, practical, voluntary, and problem-oriented.

qs.q: What term describes local community leaders who influence the agricultural opinions and adoption behaviors of fellow villagers?
qs.e: Opinion leaders are trusted informal community figures whose endorsement accelerates technology diffusion.

qs.q: What step in the adoption process involves mentally weighing the advantages and risks of an innovation before field testing?
qs.e: In the Evaluation stage, the farmer mentally assesses 'Can I do it?' and 'Will it pay?' before trying it.

qs.q: What extension technique organizes intensive short-term multimedia public campaigns to solve urgent agricultural crises like locust outbreaks?
qs.e: Mass extension campaigns deploy multi-channel communications (radio, posters, rallies) for rapid emergency action.

qs.q: What term describes the lateral spread of an innovation from adopting farmers to neighboring farmers through informal social networks?
qs.e: Diffusion is the process by which an innovation spreads over time among members of a social system through informal channels.

qs.q: What is the primary function of the omasum in the ruminant digestive tract?
o: Absorption of water and volatile fatty acids from chyme
Enzymatic digestion of proteins by pepsin
Microbial breakdown of cellulose and hemicellulose
Storage of undigested hardware and stones
qs.e: The omasum (manyplies) possesses leaf-like mucosal folds that absorb water, bicarbonate, and residual volatile fatty acids.

qs.q: What term describes non-ruminant herbivores like rabbits that digest cellulose in an enlarged cecum?
qs.e: Rabbits and horses are hindgut fermenters utilizing an enlarged cecum and colon for microbial fiber fermentation.

qs.q: What physiological practice in rabbits involves ingesting soft cecal night pellets to absorb microbial B-vitamins and protein?
qs.e: Caecotrophy (coprophagy) is the re-ingestion of nutrient-rich cecal pellets directly from the anus to maximize nutrient recovery.

qs.q: Which sheep breed in West Africa has long pendulous ears and a piebald black-and-white coat pattern?
qs.e: Uda sheep are large hair sheep native to the Sahelian zone with distinctive convex heads and piebald coats.

qs.q: Which hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland stimulates milk synthesis in female livestock mammaries?
qs.e: Prolactin initiates and maintains milk secretion within alveolar cells of the mammary gland.

qs.q: Which hormone released from the posterior pituitary gland triggers milk let-down in response to suckling stimuli?
qs.e: Oxytocin causes contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding mammary alveoli, forcing milk into teat cisterns.

qs.q: Which enzyme present in the abomasum of young suckling calves coagulates milk protein (casein)?
qs.e: Rennin curdles milk proteins in young ruminants, delaying passage and improving digestion.

qs.q: Which non-protein nitrogen (NPN) compound can be fed to adult ruminants as a cheap source of nitrogen for microbial protein synthesis?
qs.e: Rumen microbes hydrolyze urea into ammonia, using it to synthesize microbial amino acids and proteins.

qs.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes polyneuritis and curled-toe paralysis in chicks?
qs.e: Riboflavin (B2) deficiency causes nerve sheath degeneration resulting in characteristic curled-toe paralysis.

qs.q: Which essential amino acid is typically the first limiting amino acid in maize-based poultry diets?
qs.e: Maize protein is deficient in lysine and tryptophan; lysine is usually the first limiting amino acid.

qs.q: What anti-nutritional factor present in raw soybean seeds inhibits pancreatic trypsin enzyme activity?
qs.e: Raw soybeans contain heat-labile trypsin inhibitors that impair protein digestion unless toasted.

qs.q: What toxic polyphenolic compound present in unrefined cottonseed meal limits its inclusion in monogastric diets?
qs.e: Free gossypol in cottonseed meal binds iron and causes toxicity and yolk discoloration in monogastrics.

qs.q: Which antinutritional chemical compound in raw cassava peels yields toxic hydrocyanic acid upon hydrolysis?
qs.e: Linamarin and lotaustralin in raw cassava release lethal hydrocyanic acid (HCN) unless processed by drying/fermentation.

qs.q: What term describes the energy remaining after deducting energy lost in feces from gross feed energy?
qs.e: Digestible Energy (DE) = Gross Energy (GE) - Fecal Energy loss.

qs.q: Which vitamin synthesized by rumen microbes prevents pernicious anemia in cattle when cobalt is present?
qs.e: Rumen bacteria require trace cobalt to synthesize Vitamin B12 essential for red blood cell formation.

qs.q: Which mineral deficiency causes grass tetany (staggers) in lactating cattle grazing lush spring pastures?
qs.e: Hypomagnesemia (grass tetany) results from low blood magnesium levels when grazing fast-growing green pastures.

qs.q: Which water-soluble vitamin is synthesized in adequate amounts by farm animals (except primates and guinea pigs)?
qs.e: Most farm livestock synthesize Vitamin C internally from glucose in the liver or kidneys.

qs.q: Which organic acid is added to high-moisture grain to inhibit mold growth during storage?
qs.e: Propionic acid serves as an effective antifungal preservative for wet feed grains.

qs.q: Which metabolic disorder is caused by severe blood calcium drop (hypocalcemia) shortly after calving?
qs.e: Milk fever results from sudden calcium drain into colostrum, causing muscle weakness and recumbency.

qs.q: What digestive disorder results from gas accumulation trapped in stable foam inside the rumen?
qs.e: Frothy bloat occurs when soluble proteins in lush legumes form stable foam that traps microbial gases.

qs.q: What medium is used to store frozen bull semen straws at minus 196 degrees Celsius in cryogenic containers?
qs.e: Liquid nitrogen (-196 °C) maintains viable frozen semen indefinitely without cellular degradation.

qs.q: What term describes a male animal with one or both testicles retained inside the abdominal cavity?
qs.e: Cryptorchidism occurs when testicles fail to descend into the scrotum, causing infertility due to body heat.

qs.q: Which mechanized spraying structure uses pipe arches and nozzles to spray acaricide on cattle walking through a chute?
qs.e: A spray race pumps pressurized acaricide through nozzle rings as cattle walk through an enclosed alley.

qs.q: What tool is used to administer solid medicine boluses or tablets down the throat of cattle?
qs.e: A balling gun places solid pills or boluses at the back of the pharynx for forced swallowing.

qs.q: What management practice transfers piglets from large litters to foster sows with smaller litters?
qs.e: Cross-fostering balances litter sizes within 24-48 hours after farrowing to ensure all piglets get teats.

qs.q: What tool clips sharp needle teeth in newborn piglets to prevent teat damage to lactating sows?
qs.e: Piglet tooth clippers snip the 8 sharp canine and corner incisor teeth (needle teeth) shortly after birth.

qs.q: What management practice involves separating newborn calves from cows immediately after birth and hand-rearing them?
qs.e: Dairy operations separate calves early to maximize milk harvest, feeding calves colostrum and milk from buckets.

qs.q: What parameter measures the time period between consecutive calvings in a cow?
qs.e: Calving interval is the elapsed time (ideally 12-13 months) between one calving and the next.

qs.q: What technique flushes fertilized embryos from donor females and transfers them into synchronized surrogate mothers?
qs.e: Embryo transfer collects viable early embryos from valuable donor females and implants them into surrogate recipients.

qs.q: What is the primary purpose of a bull string or teaser bull fitted with a vasectomy or chin-ball marker?
o: Detecting cows in heat without fertilizing them
Increasing milk yield in lactating cows
Promoting twin births in beef herds
qs.e: Vasectomized teaser bulls mount heat cows, marking them for artificial insemination without impregnating them.

qs.q: What management operation removes the comb of young chicks to prevent frostbite and mechanical injuries?
qs.e: Dubbing clips the fleshy comb from day-old chicks or breeding roosters.

qs.q: What term describes surgical or chemical castration of young male chickens raised for tender meat?
qs.e: Caponization removes male chicken testes, producing docility, slow growth, and tender, fatty capon meat.

qs.q: Which part of the hen oviduct secretes thick and thin white albumen around the egg yolk over approximately 3 hours?
qs.e: The magnum is the longest oviduct segment, secreting raw albumen proteins around the yolk.

qs.q: Which segment of the hen oviduct secretes inner and outer shell membranes around the egg over 1.25 hours?
qs.e: The isthmus synthesizes soft fibrous inner and outer shell membranes.

qs.q: Which section of the hen reproductive tract catches the ovulated yolk from the ovary and serves as the site of fertilization?
qs.e: The infundibulum engulfs the ovulated yolk; fertilization must occur here within 15 minutes of ovulation.

qs.q: What management practice uses artificial light timers in laying houses to prevent seasonal drops in egg yield?
qs.e: Supplementary lighting extends natural day length to 16 hours, maintaining pituitary stimulation.

qs.q: Which poultry species requires the longest artificial incubation period of 35 days?
qs.e: Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) eggs take 35 days to hatch, compared to 28 days for Pekin ducks.

qs.q: Which viral disease attacks the Bursa of Fabricius in young chicks aged 3 to 6 weeks, causing immunosuppression?
o: Gumboro disease or Infectious Bursal Disease
qs.e: Infectious Bursal Disease (IBD/Gumboro) damages the Bursa of Fabricius, destroying B-lymphocytes.

qs.q: Which viral disease causes leg paralysis ('floppy leg') and tumors in nerves and visceral organs of poultry?
qs.e: Marek's disease (herpesvirus) causes T-cell lymphomas and peripheral nerve enlargement leading to leg paralysis.

qs.q: Which viral disease causes warty nodular lesions on unfeathered skin areas (comb, wattles) and diptheritic membranes in the throat?
qs.e: Fowl pox virus causes dry pox lesions on combs/wattles and wet pox diphtheritic membranes in the mouth.

qs.q: Which bacterial pathogen causes Fowl Typhoid characterized by bronze-liver lesions and high mortality?
qs.e: Salmonella gallinarum causes septicaemic Fowl Typhoid in adult poultry, turning livers dark bronze.

qs.q: Which bacterial pathogen causes Pullorum disease (bacillary white diarrhea) in young chicks?
qs.e: Salmonella pullorum causes Pullorum disease, transmitted transovarially and producing chalky white diarrhea in chicks.

qs.q: Which bacterial disease of cattle causes swelling, gas crepitation in heavy thigh muscles, and sudden lameness?
qs.e: Clostridium chauvoei causes Blackquarter, characterized by emphysematous crackling swellings in thigh muscles.

qs.q: Which bacterial pathogen causes bovine tuberculosis, producing granulomatous nodular tubercles in lungs and lymph nodes?
qs.e: Mycobacterium bovis causes chronic tuberculosis with nodular caseous lesions in pulmonary lymph nodes.

qs.q: Which tick-borne protozoan parasite infects red blood cells of cattle, causing Babesiosis or Redwater disease?
qs.e: Babesia bigemina causes intravascular hemolysis, leading to hemoglobinuria (red urine) and fever.

qs.q: Which tick species is the primary vector of Babesia bigemina and Anaplasma marginale in West Africa?
qs.e: Boophilus ticks transmit Babesia and Anaplasma species during blood feeding.

qs.q: Which mud snail species serves as the essential intermediate host for liver fluke (Fasciola species) development?
qs.e: Lymnaea species snails host larval miracidia which develop into infectious cercariae on wet pastures.

qs.q: Which cestode tapeworm infects humans as definitive hosts, using cattle as intermediate hosts containing bladder worms (cysticerci)?
qs.e: Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) forms Cysticercus bovis in bovine muscle tissue ingested by humans.

qs.q: Which cestode tapeworm uses pigs as intermediate hosts containing Cysticercus cellulosae cysts in pork?
qs.e: Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) forms measly pork cysts in swine muscle.

qs.q: Which stomach wireworm nematode sucks blood in the abomasum of sheep, causing severe anemia and bottle jaw swelling?
qs.e: Haemonchus contortus (barber's pole worm) sucks blood in the abomasum, causing severe anemia and submandibular edema.

qs.q: Which fungal pathogen causes ringworm in cattle, producing circular hairless scaly lesions on skin?
qs.e: Trichophyton verrucosum is a dermatophyte fungus causing crusty, circular ringworm lesions on cattle skin.

qs.q: Which fungal pathogen causes brooder pneumonia in young chicks exposed to moldy litter?
qs.e: Inhaled Aspergillus fumigatus spores cause granulomatous lung nodules and gasping in chicks.

qs.q: Which viral disease of pigs causes high fever, cyanotic skin blueness, internal hemorrhage, and near 100 percent mortality?
qs.e: African Swine Fever (Asfarviridae) is a highly contagious, hemorrhagic viral disease of domestic pigs.

qs.q: Which tick-borne rickettsial organism causes Anaplasmosis (gall sickness) in cattle?
qs.e: Anaplasma marginale infects bovine erythrocytes, causing severe anemia, jaundice, and fever.

qs.q: Which mycoplasmal disease affects goats, causing pleuropneumonia, high fever, and painful coughing?
qs.e: Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP) is caused by Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae.

qs.q: What parameter describes a disease that occurs consistently at low levels within an animal population?
qs.e: An enzootic disease is the animal equivalent of endemic, persisting regularly within a livestock population.

qs.q: Which diagnostic test uses tuberculin injected intradermally into cattle skin to detect bovine tuberculosis infection?
qs.e: The tuberculin test measures delayed-type hypersensitivity skin swelling 72 hours after intradermal tuberculin injection.

qs.q: Which diagnostic field test detects subclinical mastitis in dairy cows by measuring gel formation in milk samples mixed with reagent?
qs.e: The California Mastitis Test (CMT) reacts with somatic cell DNA in milk, forming a thick gel in infected quarters.

qs.q: What is the desirable pH range for well-preserved, high-quality grass silage?
qs.e: Lactic acid accumulation lowers silage pH to 3.8 - 4.2, preserving nutrients and inhibiting putrefactive bacteria.

qs.q: Which creeping legume species is known as Kudzu and is valued for smothering weeds and soil conservation?
qs.e: Pueraria phaseoloides (Tropical Kudzu) forms dense, deep mats that control soil erosion and supply nitrogen.

qs.q: What parameter defines one Tropical Livestock Unit (TLU) equivalent in livestock live weight standards?
qs.e: One Tropical Livestock Unit (TLU) is conventionally standardized as a mature bovine weighing 250 kg.

qs.q: Which rotational grazing variation uses a movable electric wire fence advanced daily to allocate narrow strips of pasture?
qs.e: Strip grazing uses portable fences moved daily to give livestock access to fresh forage strips, maximizing utilization.

qs.q: What management practice delays grazing on specific pasture paddocks until forage grass seeds mature and disperse naturally?
qs.e: Deferred grazing postpones stocking until mature grass seeds drop, rejuvenating depleted pastures naturally.

qs.q: Which grass species is known as Rhodes grass and is cultivated for hay production in sub-humid tropics?
qs.e: Chloris gayana (Rhodes grass) is a stoloniferous perennial grass widely grown for hay.

qs.q: What condition in silage indicates aerobic spoilage and activity of putrefactive Clostridia bacteria?
o: Dark slimy appearance with foul butyric acid or ammonia odor
Bright green colour with pleasant sweet-sour lactic smell
Dry golden yellow texture with zero odor
qs.e: Air ingress allows Clostridia to produce foul-smelling butyric acid and break down proteins into toxic amines.

qs.q: Which pasture grass is known as carpet grass and thrives in shaded, moist tropical soils?
qs.e: Axonopus compressus (broadleaf carpet grass) is a creeping perennial grass tolerant of shade and acid soils.

qs.q: What parameter measures the percentage of grazed herbage actually ingested by animals relative to total herbage produced?
qs.e: Utilization efficiency measures the fraction of produced forage mass consumed by grazing stock.

qs.q: Which insect pest causes severe damage to stored cowpea grains by boring holes and laying eggs inside?
qs.e: Callosobruchus maculatus (cowpea storage beetle) is the principal pest of stored cowpeas in West Africa.

qs.q: Which grain legume undergoes pegging, where the fertilized flower stalk grows downward into the soil to form pods?
qs.e: Arachis hypogaea (groundnut) forms pegs after fertilization that bend and push into the soil where pods develop underground.

qs.q: What is the processing step used to remove the fibrous outer husk from harvested cotton bolls?
qs.e: Ginning separates lint cotton fibers from the cotton seeds after harvesting.

qs.q: What is the standard moisture content required for safe long-term storage of maize grains in grain silos?
qs.e: Maize grains must be dried to 12-13% moisture content to prevent fungal growth, mold, and grain heating in silos.

qs.q: Which fiber crop is grown for producing gunny bags, twines, and coarse textiles?
qs.e: Kenaf (Hibiscus cannabinus) yields strong bast fibers used for sacking, twine, and carpet backing.

qs.q: Which processing method is used to extract palm kernel oil from cracked palm nut kernels?
qs.e: Palm kernels are crushed and subjected to mechanical screw pressing or chemical solvent extraction to yield palm kernel oil.

qs.q: Which oil seed crop produces seeds with high oil content used in making margarine and cooking oil?
qs.e: Sesamum indicum (sesame/beniseed) contains about 50% edible oil rich in antioxidants.

qs.q: What practice is required during oil palm seedling nursery management to select vigorous plants?
qs.e: Nursery culling removes deformed, diseased, or stunted seedlings before field transplanting.

qs.q: Which beverage crop is grown commercially at higher altitudes in West Africa and produces beans containing caffeine?
qs.e: Coffea arabica thrives at cool, higher elevations (1,000-2,000 m) producing high-quality coffee beans.

qs.q: Which leguminous pulse crop is grown for its seeds which contain about 40 percent crude protein and 20 percent oil?
qs.e: Glycine max (soybean) seeds contain ~40% protein and ~20% oil, making it an exceptional feed protein source.

qs.q: Which management practice prevents lodging in tall cereal crops during high wind storms?
o: Earthing up soil around base of stems
qs.e: Earthing up mounds soil around crop bases, reinforcing root anchorage and reducing wind lodging.

qs.q: Which crop yields edible underground swollen stem tubers with eyes containing vegetative buds?
qs.e: Solanum tuberosum (Irish potato) forms stem tubers bearing 'eyes' (nodes) used for propagation.

qs.q: Which agricultural crop is classified as a biennial crop under natural growth conditions?
qs.e: Daucus carota (carrot) grows vegetatively in year one and flowers/seeds in year two under temperate conditions.

qs.q: Crops cultivated specifically to lure insect pests away from main cash crops are termed:
qs.e: Trap crops are planted around main fields to attract and concentrate pests away from primary crops.

qs.q: Which crop is classified as a forage legume cultivated for livestock pasture?
qs.e: Centrosema pubescens (Centro) is a high-protein pasture legume.

qs.q: Fast-growing crops planted to utilize land temporary vacant between major crop seasons are called:
qs.e: Catch crops mature rapidly to fill seasonal gaps in field cropping schedules.

qs.q: Which family does the cassava crop (Manihot esculenta) belong to?
qs.e: Cassava belongs to the spurge family, Euphorbiaceae.

qs.q: Which plant species is classified as a root tuber crop?
qs.e: Cassava produces true root tubers derived from swollen adventitious roots.

qs.q: Which plant species produces edible subterranean stem tubers?
qs.e: Irish potato (Solanum tuberosum) forms stem tubers on stolons.

qs.q: Which agronomic classification includes crops planted to shade and protect delicate young seedlings of plantation crops?
qs.e: Nurse crops (e.g., plantain grown with young cocoa) provide temporary shade and microclimate protection.

qs.q: Which plant is classified as a medicinal or pharmaceutical crop in West Africa?
qs.e: Azadirachta indica (Neem tree) yields extracts used for medicinal and biopesticidal properties.

qs.q: Which botanical family includes cabbage, kale, and radish?
qs.e: Brassicaceae (Cruciferae) includes cole crops like cabbage, kale, and turnip.

qs.q: Which plant species is classified as a green manure legume?
qs.e: Crotalaria juncea (sunn hemp) is grown as a green manure and cover crop.

qs.q: What is the primary function of the rootstock in fruit tree grafting operations?
o: Determining fruit flavor and flower colour
Providing anchorage, root uptake, and disease resistance
Suppressing all shoot growth above ground
qs.e: Rootstock provides the root system, imparting hardiness, soil adaptability, and root disease resistance.

qs.q: What propagation method involves inducing roots on an aerial branch while still attached to the parent plant?
qs.e: Air layering (marcotting) girdles a branch bark and wraps it with moist medium to induce rooting before detachment.

qs.q: Which specialized horizontal stem grows along the soil surface and produces adventitious roots at nodes, as seen in strawberries?
qs.e: Runners (stolons) creep horizontally on the soil surface, forming new plantlets at nodes.

qs.q: What term describes breaking seed coat dormancy mechanically by scratching, nicking, or acid treatment?
qs.e: Scarification weakens or ruptures hard impermeable seed coats to permit water absorption and germination.

qs.q: What propagation technique regenerates whole plants from small plant tissues cultured in sterile nutrient media?
qs.e: Micropropagation uses tissue explants grown in aseptic nutrient media to mass-produce disease-free clones.

qs.q: What type of seed germination brings cotyledons above the soil surface due to hypocotyl elongation?
qs.e: In epigeal germination (e.g. cowpea, castor), the hypocotyl elongates, pulling cotyledons above ground.

qs.q: In which type of germination do cotyledons remain below the soil surface while the epicotyl elongates?
qs.e: In hypogeal germination (e.g. maize, broad bean), cotyledons stay underground as the epicotyl pushes shoot upward.

qs.q: What factor causes physical seed dormancy in many tropical legume seeds?
o: Impermeable hard seed coat preventing water imbibition
High concentration of gibberellins in endosperm
qs.e: Hard seed coat dormancy prevents water entry required to trigger metabolic processes for germination.

qs.q: Which plant structure is modified to form a protective bulb scale leaf?
qs.e: Bulb scales are concentric fleshy modified leaf bases storing water and nutrients.

qs.q: Which organ of perennation is a modified vertical underground stem stem-base swollen with food reserves?
qs.e: A corm is a solid, swollen vertical underground stem base with distinct nodes and internodes.

qs.q: What term refers to the embryonic shoot portion located above the cotyledonary node?
qs.e: The epicotyl is the region of the embryonic stem above cotyledon attachment that develops into true leaves and stems.

qs.q: Which plant species forms small bulbils in leaf axils used for vegetative propagation?
qs.e: Dioscorea bulbifera (aerial yam) forms bulbils in leaf axils that serve as vegetative propagation units.

qs.q: What is the term for seedless fruit development occurring without fertilization?
qs.e: Parthenocarpy is the production of fruit without fertilization, resulting in seedless fruits (e.g. commercial banana).

qs.q: What is the primary function of grafting wax applied over a newly completed graft joint?
o: Supplying inorganic nitrogen directly to scion leaves
Attracting pollinating bees to graft zone
Sealing the graft union to prevent moisture loss and infection
qs.e: Grafting wax seals cut tissues against desiccation and excludes pathogen entry until cambial fusion occurs.

qs.q: Which pruning method involves cutting back branches to ground level to stimulate new basal shoot growth?
qs.e: Coppicing cuts tree stems near ground level, stimulating vigorous sprout regeneration from basal buds.

qs.q: What is the term for cutting off the terminal growing tip of a stem to encourage lateral branching?
qs.e: Pinching removes the apical bud, overcoming apical dominance and promoting lateral shoot growth.

qs.q: What calculation determines the quantity of seed required to plant one hectare at a given spacing and seed weight?
